That very Shambhu—the giver of boons, the direct witness of every action in the universe—asks for your daughter's hand, using us as his messengers and our words as his own.
You should unite your daughter with him, just as speech is united with its meaning. Indeed, a daughter given in marriage to a worthy husband is no cause for grief to her father.
Since the Lord (Shiva) is the father of the world, all beings, both stationary and moving, will regard her as their mother.
After bowing to Shiva, the gods will then bow to her, coloring her feet with the brilliant rays emanating from the jewels on their crowns.
Uma is the bride, you are the giver, we are the supplicants, and Shambhu is the groom. Indeed, this entire arrangement is perfectly suited for the exaltation of your lineage.

Through the sacred bond of your daughter's marriage, become the elder (father-in-law) to the Teacher of the Universe—He who praises none, is praised by all, is worthy of veneration, and venerates no other.
As the divine sage (Angiras) spoke these words, Parvati, standing by her father's side with her face downcast in modesty, began to count the petals of the lotus she held in her hand.

Although his own wish was fulfilled, the Mountain (Himalaya) looked towards Menā's face for her consent. For it is common practice that in matters concerning a daughter, householders look to their wives for the final word.
Menā, too, accepted it all as her husband's desired course of action. For devoted wives are always unwavering in their support of their husband's wishes.

Reflecting that this was the proper response, Himalaya, at the conclusion of the sages' speech, took his daughter, who was adorned with auspicious ornaments, by the hand (as a sign of giving her away).

(Himalaya said,) "Come, my child. You are designated as sacred alms for the Soul of the Universe. These sages are the supplicants, and through this act, the true fruit of my life as a householder has been obtained by me."
The mountain (Himalaya), having said this much to his daughter, told the sages, "This bride of the three-eyed one (Shiva) bows to all of you."
Applauding the words of the mountain, which were generous in fulfilling the desired objective, they (the sages) caused Ambika (Parvati) to prosper with blessings that would bear fruit in the future.
Arundhati placed the blushing Parvati, whose golden ear-ornament had slipped due to her respectful bow, onto her lap.
And she (Arundhati), by describing the virtues of the unparalleled bridegroom (Shiva), made Parvati's mother, who was tear-faced and distressed with affection for her daughter, free from sorrow.
Asked at that very moment by Shiva's kinsman (Himalaya) about the wedding date, those sages, clad in bark garments, named a day three days hence and departed.
Taking leave of Himalaya, and again looking at the trident-bearer (Shiva), and having informed him that the purpose was accomplished, they, permitted by him, ascended to the sky.

Even Pashupati (Shiva), eager for union with the mountain's daughter, passed those days with difficulty. Since these emotions affect even him, the all-powerful one, what other helpless person would they not disturb?

Then, during the waxing of the moon (lord of herbs) and on a lunar day endowed with the auspicious quality of Jamitra, Himalaya, accompanied by his relatives, performed the preparatory rites for his daughter's wedding.

In every house of the mountain's city, the groups of housewives were busy with auspicious wedding preparations. Due to the affection, the entire city and the inner palace seemed comparable to a single family.
That city, its main roads strewn with Kalpa-vriksha flowers and its rows of banners made of Chinese silk, shone like another heaven with the radiance of its gleaming golden archways.

Although they had a line of sons, Uma, being their only daughter whose wedding was now imminent, became a source of special joy for her parents, as if she were seen after a long time or had risen from the dead.
Blessed by all, she went from lap to lap and enjoyed one adornment after another. The affection of the mountain's clan, though divided among many relatives, found its single focus in her.

At the Maitra muhurta, when the moon was in conjunction with the Uttara Phalguni constellation, the female relatives who were blessed with husbands and sons performed the ceremonial decoration on her body.

She adorned her ceremonial bathing attire, which was a silk garment from the Navel-country, accompanied by an arrow, and whose color was contrasted by Durva grass shoots mixed with white mustard seeds.
The young maiden, having come into contact with the new ceremonial arrow, shone like a crescent of the moon at the end of the dark fortnight, being kindled by a ray of the sun.

The women led her, who had the oil removed from her body with a paste of Lodhra, whose limbs were anointed with dried sandalwood paste, and who was wearing clothes suitable for the ceremonial bath, towards the bathing platform.

On this platform, whose surface was paved with Vaidurya gems and decorated with patterns of unpierced pearls, the women, pouring water from golden pitchers, bathed her to the accompaniment of musical instruments.

With her body purified by the auspicious bath and having put on the garment to be worn when meeting her husband, she shone like the earth, which, with its Kasha flowers in full bloom, has just received the rain from the clouds.
And from that place, she was led by chaste women, holding her, to the center of the ceremonial altar, which had a canopy, was furnished with four jeweled pillars, and had a seat prepared.
The women seated before her, having placed the slender maiden there facing east, paused for a moment. Even though the cosmetics were at hand, their eyes were captivated by her natural beauty.

One of the women bound her hair, which had been dried by the heat of incense, had flowers woven within, and was elegantly arranged, with a garland of pale Madhuka flowers intertwined with Durva grass.
They decorated her limbs with white aloe-wood paste and drew leaf-patterns with Gorochana pigment. She then surpassed the beauty of the Ganga, whose sandbanks are marked by Chakravaka birds.
The beauty of her face, with its well-arranged curls, surpassed the lotus with bees clinging to it and the disc of the moon with its streak of cloud, thus ending any talk of comparison.

A barley shoot, placed on her ear, attracted all eyes because it attained supreme beauty on her cheek, which was slightly rough from Lodhra powder and extremely fair from the application of Gorochana.

Of the well-proportioned maiden, the lower lip, defined by a line, its color slightly enhanced by beeswax, and about to attain the fruit of perfect loveliness, gained an indescribable beauty through its gentle throbbing.

A friend jokingly told Parvati, "Touch your husband's crescent moon on his head with this foot." After her feet were colored and she was blessed, Parvati, without a word, playfully struck that friend with a garland.

Her attendants, observing her eyes which were as beautiful as the petals of a well-grown lotus, did not apply black collyrium. They considered it merely an auspicious ritual, not something needed to enhance the inherent special beauty of her eyes.
As she was being adorned with ornaments, she shone like a creeper with blossoming flowers, like the night with rising stars, and like a river with settling birds.
Seeing her own radiant reflection in the mirror, the long-eyed Parvati became eager to go to Shiva. Indeed, for women, the true purpose of dressing up is to be seen by their beloved.

Then, her mother Menā, taking moist, auspicious yellow orpiment and red arsenic with her fingers, lifted up Parvati's face, which was adorned with a pure ivory ear-ornament. (This verse continues into the next).

The very first wish that had grown in Menā's heart along with the budding of her daughter Uma's youth—that wish she now, with deep emotion, transformed into the auspicious tilaka mark for the marriage ceremony on her daughter's forehead.

With eyes full of tears, Menā also tied the auspicious woolen marriage thread on her daughter's wrist. The thread, being adjusted by the nurse's fingers, was placed at a spot different from its usual position due to her emotional state.
Dressed in a new silk garment and holding a mirror, she shone even more brightly. She looked like the shore of the milk ocean with its masses of foam, and like an autumn night graced by a full moon.

The mother, Menā, who was skilled in directing ceremonies, first had Parvati, the family's honor, bow to the worshipped family deities. Then, she had her sequentially touch the feet of the virtuous, married women present.

As Uma bowed, the women blessed her, saying, "May you receive the unbroken love of your husband." However, for her, who was destined to become half of Shiva's body, even these heartfelt blessings from loved ones seemed secondary.

The accomplished and courtly Mountain King, Himalaya, having completed all the preparations for his daughter's wedding in a manner befitting her wishes and his own stature, stood in the assembly hall filled with friends and relatives, awaiting the arrival of Shiva.
Meanwhile, on Mount Kailasa, the divine Mothers, with great reverence, placed before the groom, Shiva, the chastiser of cities, adornments befitting that unprecedented wedding.

Out of respect for the divine Mothers, the Lord Shiva merely touched the splendid auspicious ornaments they offered. His own inherent attire itself, befitting the groom, attained a new and desired state of beauty.

His ash itself became the white cosmetic paste. The skull he wore became as beautiful as a pure crest-jewel. And his elephant hide, marked with yellow pigment on its edges, assumed the quality of a fine silk garment.
His third eye, shining on his forehead with its pure, tawny pupil, itself served the purpose of the auspicious tilaka mark, which is typically made of yellow orpiment.

The bodies of the serpent lords adorning Shiva, which were to be transformed into other ornaments like gold, underwent a change. However, the brilliance of their hood-jewels remained just as they were, unchanged.

For Shiva, whose crest is always adorned by the crescent moon—which shines brightly even during the day and whose dark spot is not yet visible due to its newness—what need was there to wear a separate crest-jewel?
Thus, Shiva, the sole source of wonders and the ordainer of even the established rules of attire, by his divine power, saw his own reflection in a sword brought to him by a nearby attendant.

Leaning on Nandi's arm, Shiva mounted his bull, whose broad back was covered with a tiger skin and whose massive form had been condensed out of devotion. Mounting him, who was like a moving Kailasa, Shiva set out.

Following the god Shiva, the divine Mothers, whose ear-ornaments trembled with the movement of their celestial vehicles, made the sky appear like a lake of lotuses with their faces, which were radiant like the pollen from their halos.
And behind those golden-hued Mothers shone Kali, adorned with skulls. She appeared like a line of dark clouds accompanied by cranes, with lightning flashing far ahead of it.

Then, the Ganas preceding the trident-bearer Shiva raised a clamor of auspicious music. This sound, pervading the spires of the celestial chariots, announced to the other gods that the time for rendering service had arrived.
The Sun held over Shiva a new parasol crafted by Tvashtri. With his crest close to the parasol's silk canopy, Shiva shone as if the celestial Ganga was once again descending upon his head.

At that time, the rivers Ganga and Yamuna, in personified forms, served the god by waving whisks. Even though they had abandoned their river forms, the movement of the white whisks made them appear as if they were still accompanied by flights of swans.

The first creator, Brahma, and the Supreme Being Vishnu himself, marked with the Shrivatsa, followed him. With their cries of "Victory!", they augmented his glory, just as an oblation of ghee increases a fire.

That one and the same form divided itself into three: Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. The state of being first or last among them is interchangeable. Sometimes Shiva is prior to Vishnu, sometimes Vishnu is prior to him; sometimes Brahma is prior to them both, and at other times, they are both prior to Shiva.

The guardians of the worlds, led by Indra, their attire made humble by setting aside their royal insignia, bowed down to him (Shiva) with folded hands. They had been signaled by Nandi for the audience and were shown the way by him.

He (Shiva) honored them according to their rank: Brahma, the lotus-born, with a nod of his head; Vishnu with a word; Indra, the slayer of Vritra, with a smile; and all the remaining gods with a mere glance.

The Seven Sages in front of him uttered blessings of victory. He (Shiva) then spoke to them with a smile, saying, "In this extensive marriage-sacrifice, you have been previously chosen by me as the Adhvaryu priests."

The wearer of the crescent moon (Shiva), whose heroic deed of destroying the three cities was being sung by skilled Gandharvas led by Vishvavasu, traversed the path, being one who could easily overcome the darkness and other obstacles of the journey.

In the sky, his playfully-moving mount (Nandi), adorned with jingling golden bells, carried him. It repeatedly shook its two horns, on which clouds were impaled, as if to shake off mud stuck from striking a riverbank.

He reached the city, protected by the lord of mountains and unassailed by enemies, in a moment, as if being pulled along by golden threads, which were in fact his own eager glances fixed ahead of him.

Near that city, the god whose throat is dark like a cloud, watched by the citizens with upturned faces full of curiosity, descended from his path in the sky (marked by his arrow) and approached the surface of the earth.

The emperor of mountains (Himalaya), delighted by his arrival, went forth to receive him. He was accompanied by herds of elephants mounted by his prosperous relatives, appearing like his own mountain slopes adorned with blossoming trees.

The two groups, that of the gods and that of the mountains' retinue, their clamor spreading far, met at the city gate whose doors were opened, just like two torrents of water meeting after breaking a single dam.

The mountain lord (Himalaya) felt shy when Shiva, who is revered by the three worlds, bowed to him. Indeed, previously, overwhelmed by Shiva's greatness, he had not even been aware of his own head bowing low before him.

With his face beaming with joy, he (Himalaya), assuming the role of the son-in-law's guide, led him (Shiva) into the magnificent palace, the market streets of which were strewn with flowers up to the ankles.
At that moment, on the rows of palaces, the actions of the beautiful women of the city, who were eager to see Ishana (Shiva) and had abandoned all other tasks, were as follows.
As one woman hurried to a window, the garland fell from her untied hair. Though she tried to hold her mass of hair with her hand, she could not manage to tie it up.

Another woman, pulling back her foot which was held by her attendant for applying lac-dye, ran with the wet dye still on it. Abandoning her graceful gait, she created a trail of red footprints all the way to the window.
Another woman, having adorned her right eye with collyrium but leaving the left one undone, went to the vicinity of the window just like that, still carrying the applicator stick.

Another woman, her gaze fixed through a lattice window, did not tie her girdle-knot which had come loose in her haste. She stood there, holding up her garment with one hand, the radiance of whose ornaments shone upon her navel.
At that time, the girdle of a certain woman who had risen in a hurry, being only half-strung, slipped at every unsteady step, until only the thread held by her big toe remained.

The windows, with their spaces filled by the faces of those intensely curious women, seemed to be adorned with lotuses. Their faces were fragrant with wine, and their restless eyes were like hovering bees.

Meanwhile, the moon-crested one (Shiva) entered the royal road, which was filled with flags and adorned with arches. His radiance made the palace tops doubly bright, as if bathed in moonlight even during the day.

The women, drinking him in with their eyes as the sole object of sight, did not perceive any other sensory objects. For it was as if the functions of all their other senses had completely entered their eyes.

"It is fitting that even the delicate Aparna (Parvati) performed severe penance for him. Any woman who could attain even servitude to him would be fulfilled; what then to say of one who attains a place on his lap?"
"If the Creator had not united this pair, whose beauty is mutually desirable, then his entire effort in fashioning the beauty in these two would have been fruitless."

"Surely, the body of the flower-arrowed one (Kamadeva) was not burnt by him in a fit of anger. I think that upon seeing this god, Kama himself, out of shame at his own inferior beauty, abandoned his body."

"Oh friend! Having fortunately formed a relationship with this lord, who was sought after by her heart's desire, the king of mountains will now hold his head, already high from supporting the earth, even higher."

Listening to the ear-pleasing conversations of the women of Oshadhiprastha, the three-eyed Shiva reached the abode of Himalaya, where handfuls of parched grains were being crushed by the armlets of the welcoming crowd.

There, having dismounted from his bull with a hand lent by Achyuta (Vishnu), Shiva, resembling the sun emerging from an autumn cloud, entered the inner apartments of the lord of mountains, which had been previously traversed by the lotus-seated Brahma.

The gods led by Indra, the great sages preceded by the Saptarshis, and Shiva's attendants all followed him and entered the mountain's abode, just as those with a noble purpose follow a laudable beginning.

There, Lord Shiva, having taken his seat, duly accepted everything offered by the Mountain (Himalaya)—the respectful offering (arghya) with jewels, the madhuparka, and two new silk garments—all without the recitation of mantras.
Clad in silk garments, he (Shiva) was led near the bride by the courteous palace guards, just as the ocean, with its distinct lines of foam, is drawn towards the shore by the new rays of the moon.
United with the maiden Parvati, whose face shone with the brilliance of a full moon, Shiva became like the world in autumn: his eyes bloomed like water lilies, and his mind became clear like water.
At that moment, as their gazes met, their eyes—timid, flickering towards each other, slightly fixed and then withdrawn—experienced the constraint of shyness.

The eight-formed Shiva took her red-fingered hand, offered by her father, the great mountain, as if it were the first sprout of the bodiless Kama, who, suspecting this union, was secretly hiding in Uma's body.
On Uma, horripilation appeared. The bull-bannered one (Shiva) had perspiring fingers. Through the union of their hands, the influence of the mind-born Kama seemed to be equally divided between them.

If any other bride and groom, having performed the hand-taking ceremony, attain excellent beauty, then what can be said of the splendor of both (the ceremony and the couple) due to the proximity of these two (Shiva and Parvati)?
As that couple circumambulated the high-flaming fire from left to right, they shone like the inseparable pair of Day and Night revolving around the slopes of Mount Meru.

After leading the couple thrice around the fire, the priest had the bride—her eyes closed from the touch of her husband's fingertips—perform the offering of parched grains into that brightly blazing fire.

Following the priest's instruction, she (Parvati) brought the handful of fragrant smoke from the parched grains towards her face. That smoke, its wisp curling over her cheek, momentarily assumed the role of a blue lotus ear-ornament.

From inhaling the ritual smoke, the bride's face became slightly moist with a reddish hue on her cheeks, the black collyrium in her eyes was smudged by her tears, and the barley-shoot ear-ornament wilted.
The priest addressed the bride: "My child, this fire is the primary witness to your marriage. Without any hesitation, you must perform your righteous duties together with your husband, Shiva."

Bhavani (Parvati), stretching her ears to the corners of her eyes, drank in those words of her preceptor, just as the earth, scorched by the intense heat of summer, drinks the first waters of Indra (the first rain).
Urged by her handsome and steadfast husband to look at the pole star (Dhruva), she, with her voice choked by shyness, lifted her face and somehow managed to say, "I have seen it."
Thus, with the wedding ceremonies conducted by the ritual-knowing priest, the two, the parents of all beings, bowed down to the great father (Brahma) seated on his lotus throne.

The Creator (Brahma) blessed the bride, saying, "O blessed one, may you be the mother of a hero." Although he was the lord of speech, after blessing the eight-formed one (Shiva), he became still with thought.

Afterwards, the husband and wife, approaching the prepared square altar and seated on a golden throne, experienced the customary and desirable worldly ritual of placing wet, unbroken rice grains on each other.
Lakshmi held a lotus-parasol over the couple. Its long stalk served as the handle, and with clusters of water drops clinging to the petal edges, it rivaled the beauty of a net of pearls.

Saraswati also praised the couple with speech employed in two ways: she praised the excellent groom with words purified by sacred tradition (Vedic chants), and the bride with compositions that were sweet and easy to understand (secular poetry).

For a while, the couple watched the first performance of the Apsaras, a dance characterized by graceful movements, varied styles in its dramatic junctures, and melodies appropriate to the different sentiments (rasas) being expressed.

At the end of the performance, the gods, with hands joined in reverence above their crowns, bowed before Hara, who had now taken a wife. They requested the services of the five-arrowed one (Kama), who had regained his form at the end of his curse.

The Lord (Shiva), now free from anger, consented to the activity of Kama's arrows, even upon himself. Indeed, a request made at the right time by those who know how to act achieves success with their masters.

Then, Shiva (the moon-crested one), after dismissing the hosts of gods, took the daughter of the mountain king (Parvati) by the hand and went to the nuptial chamber, which was adorned with decorative patterns around golden pitchers and had a bed prepared on the ground.

There, Lord Shiva secretly made Gauri laugh with the distorted faces of his Pramathas. She was adorned with the shyness of a new bride, turning her face away when he tried to lift it, and was somehow still speaking to her chambermaids.

After the wedding ceremony, the body of Parvati, the mountain king's daughter, became charming with the longings of love, which arose from her acceptance of love mixed with apprehension towards Shiva.
When spoken to, she did not reply. When he held her garment, she wished to leave. She lay on the bed with her face turned away. Yet, all this was for the pleasure of Shiva (the wielder of Pinaka).
When her beloved (Shiva) pretended to be asleep, Parvati, out of curiosity, cast her gaze upon his face. But when he opened his eyes with a smile, she closed hers as if struck by lightning.
Then, with her trembling hand, she stopped Shankara's hand which was placed on her navel region. And her silk garment, its knot loosened, spontaneously fell away.
'O friend, serve Shankara in private, having controlled your apprehension.' She, agitated, did not remember this advice given by her friends when her beloved was right in front of her.

To Shiva (the chastiser of Ananga), who was keen on asking questions even about trivial matters just to start a conversation, Parvati responded. Acknowledging him with a glance, she gave her answer, which consisted of a shake of her head.
Her garment taken away, she covered Shiva's two eyes with both her hands. But as his forehead-eye was watching, she became distressed in private, her effort having been in vain.

The love-play of the bride—withholding her lips in kisses, her hands limp during a forceful embrace, and her passion restrained—was still dear to her Lord, because her reciprocation was hard to obtain.

Parvati could only endure her beloved's actions that were gentle: the seizing of her face that left her lips unbitten, the nail marks that left no wound, and the love-making that was compassionate. She could not bear anything else.
At dawn, when her friends were eager to ask about the night's events, she, out of shyness, did not make them lose their curiosity (by telling them). Yet, in her heart, she was eager to tell.
And seeing in the mirror the signs of love-making on her own body, and then seeing the reflection of her beloved who had sat down behind her, what various acts of shyness did she not perform?
Her mother (Menā), seeing her whose youth was enjoyed by the Blue-throated one (Shiva), was relieved. For a bride, by being dear to her husband, casts away her mother's mental anguish.
For some days, love-making was somehow performed by Sthanu (Shiva) and her. Gradually, having come to know the essence of passion, she gave up her painful aversion to love-play.
Pressed to his chest, she embraced her beloved. She did not turn away her face when he sought it for a kiss. She loosely restrained his hand when it moved with longing towards her girdle.
Then, in just a few days, their love grew deep and mutual. It was indicated by gestures, saw no displeasure, was full of sweet words, and was anxious at even a moment's separation.

Just as the bride grew fond of her husband who was worthy of her, so did the husband grow fond of her. Indeed, the Ganga never leaves the ocean, and he too found his sole delight in the nectar of her face.

Having accepted discipleship in private to Shankara, the instructor in the art of love, whatever feminine skill she learned from him, that very skill was made into his tutorial fee (by her practicing it on him).
Ambika (Parvati), shaking her sprout-like hand in pain, for a moment soothed her lower lip, which had been bitten and then released, with the cool crescent moon on the head of Shulin (Shiva).
Shankara, too, offered his forehead-eye, which was soiled by the powder from her hair-locks during a kiss, to her breath, which carried the fragrance of a blooming lotus, to have it cleaned.
Thus, by following the path of sensual pleasure, Vrishadhvaja (Shiva), having favored Manmatha (the god of love), lived with Uma in the palace of the mountain king for a full month.

He, the self-existent one (Shiva), after taking leave of Himavat who was distressed by the sorrow of separation from his daughter, roamed here and there, flying with his bull (Nandi) of immeasurable speed.

The accomplished one (Shiva), whose bull was as swift as the wind, went to Mount Meru. There he enjoyed beds made of arrangements of golden sprouts, which were marked by Parvati's breasts and were able to withstand the ardors of love-making.

And he, who was like a bee to the lotus of Parvati's face, also dwelt on the slopes of Mount Mandara, on the rocks marked with the footprints of Padmanabha (Vishnu), which had received fresh drops of nectar.
Frightened by the trumpeting of an elephant, Parvati tightly embraced Shiva around his neck. The preceptor of the world, Shiva, thus enjoyed the clear moonbeams on the Ekapingala mountain.

Once, while Shiva was enjoying himself in the Malaya region, the southern wind, like a flatterer, removed his beloved's fatigue. This wind, which had shaken the sandalwood creepers, was fragrant with cloves and kesara flowers.
Uma, who playfully struck her beloved Shiva with a golden lotus and whose eyes were closed by his lotus-like hands, plunged into the celestial river. A line of fish formed a second girdle around her.
While the three-eyed Shiva was adorning Parvati in the Nandana garden with Parijata flowers fit for the curls of Sachi, he was gazed at longingly for a long time by the wives of the gods.
Thus Shankara, accompanied by his beloved, having experienced both celestial and earthly pleasures, once resorted to the Gandhamadana mountain when the sunlight was turning red at sunset.
There, resting on a golden rock slab and seeing the sun within his sight, Shiva spoke to his wife and partner in dharma, Parvati, who was leaning on his left arm.

'This lord of the day, the Sun, having transferred his lotus-like splendor to the red corners of your eyes, now withdraws the day, just as the Lord of Creatures withdraws the world at the time of universal dissolution.'
'As the sun sets and its rays no longer interact with the water spray, these waterfalls of your father, the Himalaya, become devoid of the halos of rainbows.'

'For the pair of Chakravaka birds in the lake—who were holding garlands of lotus filaments, who are now crying with necks turned towards each other, and who are afflicted by separation—the small distance between them has now become vast.'
'The elephants, leaving their daily resting places fragrant from breaking Sallaki tree branches, are now taking up water—in which bees are trapped inside closed lotuses—to sustain them until dawn.'
'O you of few words, see! The sun, hanging at the edge of the western horizon, has created with its long reflection in the lake waters what looks like a golden bridge.'
'Having passed the day's heat, the tusked leaders of wild boar herds, looking as if they have bitten curved lotus-stalks, are emerging from the small, thick-mudded pond after churning it up.'

'O you with lovely thighs! This peacock, perched on the treetop with its tail-feathers spread in a circle as radiant as molten gold, seems as if it is drinking the diminishing day, whose sunlight is now fading.'

'The sky, from which the sun has removed the 'water' of its light, now appears like a lake with little water left. On one side, the east, with the spreading darkness, it seems as if the mud has become visible.'

'The hermitages now possess a special beauty, with deer entering their courtyards, small trees fresh from being watered, cows and sacred fires being brought inside, and the sacrificial fires being kindled.'
'Even though its petals are closing, the lotus remains with a slight opening for a moment, as if to lovingly give space for the bee, who is about to take up lodging, to enter.'
'The western direction, adorned from afar by the red sun whose rays are now few and countable, appears like a maiden decorated with a saffron-mixed tilaka mark of a Bandhujiva flower.'

'His companions, the Valakhilya sages who subsist on the sun's heat, praise the sun in their thousands with Sama hymns. Their voices are as pleasing as the neighing of his chariot-horses, and they praise the sun whose splendor is now infused with the glow of fire.'

'This sun, having deposited the day in the great ocean, now sets, drawn by his horses. Their necks are bent, their eyes are brushed by the chowries on their ears, and their manes are curved by the yoke.'
'With the sun having set, the sky seems asleep. Such is the fate of great energy: indeed, by as much as it rises to illuminate, by that much it must also fall to set.'

'The venerable body of the sun, placed on the peak of the setting mountain, is followed even by the twilight. How can she, who was honored by him first at sunrise, not follow him in his time of adversity?'

'O you with curly hair! See how these edges of the clouds shine, colored red, yellow, and brown. It is as if the twilight, thinking 'You will see this,' has beautifully decorated them with painter's brushes.'
'See how the sun has, as it were, distributed the evening glow upon the manes of the lions, upon the trees producing fresh blossoms, and upon the mineral-rich peaks of the mountains.'

'O daughter of the mountain king! These ascetics, who know the proper rituals, having performed their water offerings, now respectfully chant the profound Gayatri mantra at twilight for their purification.'
'O sweet-speaker! Therefore, you should permit me for a moment for the religious observance I am about to begin. Your group of friends, skilled in entertainment, will keep you amused.'
Then Parvati, the daughter of the mountain king, inclined to disregard her husband's words, bit her lip and spoke without any reason to her nearby attendant, Vijaya.
Lord Shiva, having duly performed the evening rituals preceded by mantras, approached Parvati, who was silent out of jealousy, and spoke to her again with a smile.

"O you who get angry without cause, abandon your anger! I bowed to the evening twilight, not to another woman. Don't you know me, your partner in religious duties, whose conduct is as faithful as that of a Chakravaka bird?"

"O beautiful one, that very form (Sandhya) which was previously cast off by Brahma when he created the Pitris, now attends to the sunset and sunrise. Therefore, O proud one, there is dignity for me in this act, not disgrace."
"O daughter of the mountain king, look at this twilight, now afflicted by the growing darkness. On one side, lined with Tamala trees on its bank, it appears like a river of mineral ores."
The western direction holds the evening sunlight—a red streak, the last remnant of the set sun—just as a battlefield holds a blood-stained scimitar that has been cast aside.
"O long-eyed one! As the light born from the union of night and day is obstructed by Mount Sumeru, this unrestrained, profound darkness spreads widely in all directions."
At night, this world, enveloped by a mass of darkness, exists as if in a womb. The gaze cannot move upwards, nor downwards, nor around, nor forward, nor backward.

Whatever is pure or impure, stationary or moving, crooked or endowed with straightness—all is made equal by darkness. Fie upon the greatness of the wicked, which similarly obliterates all distinctions.
"O lotus-faced one! Surely the lord of sacrificers, the moon, is rising to dispel the darkness of the night. The face of the eastern direction is covered as if with the pollen of Ketaki flowers."

The star-lit night is perceived through the moon, whose form is hidden by Mount Mandara, just as you, accompanied by your dear friend, are perceived by me from behind as if through your words being heard.

The lunar orb, whose exit was blocked until day's end and whose faint moonlight-smile was seen before, now pours forth its light, as if, prompted by the night, it is revealing a secret of the directions.

"Look! The pair of Chakravaka birds, separated by a great distance, is being imitated by the moon, whose lustre is like that of a ripe Priyangu fruit and whose reflection marks the water of the sky-lake."
"For making your ear-ornaments, it is possible to pluck the newly risen rays of the moon, the lord of herbs, which are as tender as unripe barley sprouts, with the tips of your fingernails."
The moon, grasping the darkness with its rays as if holding a mass of hair with fingers, seems to kiss the face of the night, whose eyes are like lotuses that have closed into buds.

"Look, Parvati! The surface of the sky, with its darkness partially dispelled by the rays of the new moon, appears like the Manasa lake becoming clear after being muddied by the sporting of elephants."
This moon, having abandoned its reddish hue, has become perfectly white-orbed. Indeed, in those of pure nature, any change caused by a fault of time is not long-lasting.

The light of the moon rests on high places, while the darkness of the night is intent on seeking low places. Surely, the Creator has ordained here that the course of virtues and faults should go to their likes.
The mountain, with drops of water from moonstones whose flow is caused by the moon's rays, awakens at an untimely hour those sleeping peacocks in the trees on its slopes.
"Look, beautiful one! The moon, with its rays now flickering on the tops of the Kalpa trees, seems to have become curious to count, as it were, the pearl necklaces hanging there."
This moonlight, mixed with darkness due to the unevenness of the mountain's surface, shines like the sacred ash marking applied in various patterns on a rutting elephant.
The night-lotus, having drunk the moon's nectar-like light as it bloomed, now bursts open right down to its stalk, as if unable to bear it, releasing the humming of bees.
"Look, O passionate one! A garment hanging from a Kalpa tree, its form made indistinct by the pure moonlight, is revealed only by its fluttering when the wind blows."
"It is possible to arrange your locks of hair with these moonbeams—which are lifted up from below, are as delicate as fallen flowers from the trees, and are fragmented by leaves—as if with fingers."

"O lovely-faced one! This moon is being joined with its principal star (Yogatara), which has a flickering disc, just as a bridegroom is joined with a newly initiated bride who is trembling with nervousness."
Shiva says to Parvati: "The moonlight seems to grow upon your cheeks, which are as fair as ripened reed stalks and clear with a shining reflection, as if its eye is fixed on the disc of the moon."
The presiding deity of the Gandhamadana forest, herself holding wine from the wish-fulfilling tree served in a ruby vessel, has approached you, who are full of dignity.
"O playful one, your face is fragrant with moist saffron, and your eyes are naturally red as if intoxicated. What other quality can wine, finding a home here, possibly add?"
"Or, if your friends are worthy of your respect, let this love-kindling drink be partaken." Having spoken these noble words, Shankara made Ambika drink the beverage.

Parvati underwent a transformation from consuming the drink. This change, though charming even in noble people, was like a mango tree attaining its special fragrant 'Sahakara' state, a transformation created by an inconceivable act of fate.
At that moment, as their shame vanished and passion flared, and they were about to go to bed, the beautiful-faced Parvati came under the control of two: the Trident-bearer (Shiva) and intoxication.

Ishvara (Shiva) for a long time drank in Uma's face with his eyes, not with his mouth. Her face had rolling eyes, faltering speech, and a smile caused by intoxication, adorned with beads of perspiration.

Carrying her, who was difficult to bear due to the weight of her hips and whose golden girdle was hanging loose, Ishvara, whose powers were gathered through meditation, secretly entered the jeweled chamber.

There, the lover (Shiva), accompanied by his beloved, lay upon the bed, which had a cover as white as a swan and was as beautiful to behold as a sandbank of the Ganga. He was like the Moon resting on an autumn cloud.
His lovemaking with Parvati—marked by dishevelled hair, wiped-off sandal paste, exchanged nail marks, passionate jealousy, and the snapping of her girdle's string—was not enough for his satisfaction.
As the rows of stars began to set, he, compassionate towards his beloved and holding her chest in an embrace, merely indulged in the playful curiosity of closing his eyes, not truly sleeping.

He, who is worthy of the praise of the wise, awoke at dawn simultaneously with the golden lotus ponds, serenaded by auspicious songs sung by the Kinnaras in the Kaishika raga with its melodic modulations.

The breezes from the edges of the Gandhamadana forest, which indicated the blossoming of lotuses and stirred waves of emotion in the mind, served the couple for a moment as they loosened their embrace.
At that moment, Hara (Shiva), his eyes captivated by the lines of nail marks at the base of her thighs, stopped his beloved as she was trying to fasten her loosened garment.
The passionate one (Shiva), gazing at his beloved's face—her eyes reddish from wakefulness, her lip marked by deep teeth bites, her curls dishevelled, and her tilaka mark disturbed—took delight.

At the end of the night, even though the bed was clean, he did not leave it. The bed's cover was uneven with wrinkles, the threadless girdle lay heaped in the middle, and it was marked with the lac-dye from her feet.
Desiring to enjoy day and night the nectar of his beloved's face, which produced increasing joy, he became invisible to those eager for his audience, communicating through his attendant Vijaya.

For Shambhu, constantly united with Parvati, more than a hundred seasons passed like a single night where day and night were one. Yet, his thirst for the pleasures of love was not quenched, just as the submarine fire is not extinguished by the ocean's waters.
In the midst of such amorous passion, Lord Śiva, while enjoying the lotus-like face of his beloved Pārvatī like a bee, saw a single pigeon entering the inner apartment of enjoyment.

The pigeon was cooing in a way that imitated the soft, amorous moans of lovely women. Its red eyes were rolling, its throat was repeatedly expanding, rising, and bending, and its beautiful tail was constantly lowered.
Holding its wings slightly unrestrained, the moon-colored pigeon moved here and there in circles with a joyful gait due to passion, its feet moving intricately.
Upon seeing the bird, which appeared like a fresh mass of foam rising from a heart of nectar being churned by Kāmadeva and Rati, Lord Śiva felt a moment of delight.

Observing the bird's extraordinary and divine appearance, Lord Śiva realized it was actually the fire-god Agni in disguise. Upon this recognition, he became terrible with a frown and was filled with anger.
Then Agni, assuming his true form, trembling excessively with fear and folding his hands in reverence, spoke these clear words to the enemy of Kāmadeva, Lord Śiva.
Agni addressed Śiva, stating that he is the sole Lord of the worlds and the destroyer of the gods' calamities. Therefore, harassed by the demons, the gods led by Indra seek refuge in and worship him.

Agni explains that while Śiva spent a hundred seasons in private dalliance, captivated by his love for Pārvatī, Indra and the other gods have fallen into extreme misery because they were unable to see him.

Agni states that he was requested by the gods, headed by Indra, who are waiting for a chance to serve Śiva. Therefore, he arrived in the form of a bird, suitable for the situation, to search for the Lord.
O Lord, considering this in your mind, please forgive our offense. Tell us, can those who are seeking refuge and are being oppressed by their enemies afford to tolerate any further delay in time?

The gods entreat Śiva, 'O Lord, be pleased! Quickly create a son of your own. Obtaining him as the commander of the army, Indra will regain the sovereignty of heaven and, by your grace, protect the three worlds.'
Upon hearing Agni's meaningful request, Śiva became pleased. Indeed, eloquent and beautiful words are capable of satisfying the Lord.
Śiva, the destroyer of Madana, being pleased in mind, contemplated in his heart a future course of action for the birth of the conqueror of Tārakāsura and for the victory of Indra's commander.

Then Śiva, the ascetic whose seed is drawn up, deposited that unfailing and unbearable semen—discharged due to the interruption of his amorous play—into Agni, who appeared like the fire at the end of a Yuga.
Then Agni suddenly bore his own body, which had become discolored by the deposition of Śiva's seed, appearing like a pure mirror whose surface is clouded by hot breath.

Enraged by the interruption of her sexual bliss, Pārvatī cursed Agni, saying, 'O Fire! You shall become an eater of all things, a performer of terrible deeds, afflicted by leprosy, and filled with smoke.'
Carrying a disfigured body due to the accumulation of the potent semen, Agni departed. He resembled the moon waning under Dakṣa's curse, or a lotus bud blighted by frost.
Śiva consoled Pārvatī, who was embarrassed and angry at Agni's intrusion and whose face was bowed with the bashfulness of love. He comforted her with sweet words filled with erotic sentiment.
Removing the marks of collyrium spread by heavy sweat from the spotless, moon-like face of his beloved Pārvatī, Śiva used the moving hem of his second garment to wipe it away.
With a trembling hand and tired fingers, Śiva sportively removed the perspiration from Pārvatī's lotus-like face, gently wiping it and using the breeze from a fan.

Lord Śiva, whose crest is adorned by the moon, tied Pārvatī's mass of hair which had become loosened during their amorous play and was resting on her shoulders with falling flowers. He bound her tresses using a garland made of celestial Pārijāta flowers.

The moon-faced Śiva painted decorative musk patterns on the cheeks of the beautiful Pārvatī. These patterns appeared like a series of mystical syllables from a world-deluding mantra belonging to the perfected God of Love.

Śiva placed circular earrings on both her ears. Her face appeared like the chariot of the world-conquering Kāmadeva; it seemed as if the flower-bowed god certainly mounts this chariot (her face) to achieve his victory.
Śiva placed a pearl necklace around Pārvatī's neck that draped over her breasts. This necklace possessed the beauty of two streams of the Gaṅgā flowing over the twin peaks of Mount Meru.

Śiva, the enemy of Kāmadeva, tied a girdle around Pārvatī's hips which were marked by nail-scratches. It appeared as if he were using a noose belonging to Kāmadeva to capture and bind the restless deer of his own mind.

Śiva himself prepared collyrium using the fire from his third eye and carefully applied it to Pārvatī's lotus-like eyes. He then wiped his stained finger on his own dark-blue neck, which was bristling with thrill (horripilation) at her touch.
After applying red lac dye to the tips of lotus-eyed Pārvatī's feet, the moon-crested Śiva washed the red stains from his hands using the holy waters of the Gaṅgā residing in his own matted hair.

Śiva sportively wiped the surface of a mirror against his own ash-smeared body to clean it. He then showed the mirror to his beloved Pārvatī so that she could observe the exquisite beauty of the decorations he had just adorned her with.

Looking into the jeweled mirror given by her beloved, Pārvatī noticed the marks of their union on her body. Though she felt bashful, her intense internal passion manifested outwardly under the guise of the thrills (horripilation) visible on her skin.

Beholding her beautiful decoration fashioned by her beloved Śiva in the mirror, Pārvatī smiled. Shaking off her initial bashfulness, she felt a surge of pride and considered herself to be the foremost and most fortunate among all blessed women.

Then, on that appropriate occasion, the two affectionate friends Vijayā and Jayā entered the inner chamber. They served Pārvatī, who was seated on the lap of the moon-crested Lord Śiva, with great splendor and various artistic services.

Outside, the bards loudly performed auspicious songs that were beautiful and depicted varied deeds. Meanwhile, groups of Gandharvas sang along with the sounding of conches for the delight of Lord Śiva, the wielder of the Pināka bow.

Thereafter, at the time appointed for their service, as the groups of gods were waiting intently to see the Lord, Nandī approached the door. Bowing down with folded hands, he announced their arrival to Lord Śiva.

The Great Lord Śiva, holding the hand of Pārvatī (the daughter of the Himalaya, compared here to a royal swan of the Mānasa lake), stepped out sportively from the palace of amorous play toward the waiting gods.

One by one, the gods headed by Indra bowed down with their hands folded over their heads. They paid their respects to Lord Śiva and to the Goddess Pārvatī, the daughter of the King of the Himalayas and the mother of the three worlds.

The bull-bannered Lord Śiva dismissed the gods to return as they had come, after honoring and gratifying them. Then, supported by the arm offered by Nandī, He mounted His bull along with Pārvatī and set out on His journey.

As Lord Śiva proceeded through the path of the sky on His bull, which moved with a speed exceeding that of thought, He was saluted by the dwellers of celestial chariots. These celestial beings, moving sportively for their own pleasure, honored Him with folded hands.

The celestial breeze, which wafts through the waters of the heavenly Gaṅgā and removes the fatigue of women after love-making, served the divine couple. Carrying the fragrance of Pārijāta blossoms, it fanned Pārvatī and Lord Śiva as they traveled.

Lord Śiva reached Mount Kailāsa, the king of crystal mountains, which reached into the sky. With its peaks holding the crescent moon and its winding valleys resembling serpent coils, the majestic mountain appeared as if it were a second form of the Lord Himself, who also wears the moon, snakes, and sacred ash.

On that mountain, the crystal walls are so clear that the wives of the Siddhas see their own reflections in them. Mistaking their own reflections for other women, they become jealous and stubborn in their pride, turning their faces away even as their lovers bow down to appease them.
In that crystal palace, the reflection of the moon's spots appears like a patch of musk paste applied by Pārvatī herself, owing to the brilliance of the crystal walls.
Great elephants, seeing their own bodies reflected on the crystal walls, mistake them for rival intoxicated elephants and angrily strike the walls with their tusks, suffering the pain of the impact.
At night, the celestial women (Siddha wives) see the reflections of stars in the crystal dwellings and mistake them for bright pearls scattered from their necklaces after amorous play.
The moon, which serves as a mirror for celestial ladies, appears as a priceless crest-jewel when it rests upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa, the abode of Lord Śiva.

In that place, gods longing for love gather with their beloveds in private; though they are alone, their numerous reflections on the crystal walls make them appear as if they are accompanied by a large retinue.
Lord Śiva, adorned with the crescent moon, spent a long time sporting spontaneously with Pārvatī on the crystal peaks of Kailāsa with continuous and captivating amorous gestures.
Pārvatī, looking radiantly graceful, held the hand of Lord Śiva and walked sweetly along the path shown by Nandi, who led the way carrying his staff.
Instructed by a mere hint of Śiva's eyebrow, the attendant Bhṛṅgī danced for Pārvatī's amusement, his crest shaking, his limbs moving grotesquely, showing his sharp white teeth and face.
Commissioned by the pleased Lord Śiva, Kālī, with a garland of skulls swaying on her neck and a face made fearsome by fangs, danced to delight Śiva’s beloved wife, Pārvatī.
Seeing those two fearsome attendants roaring dreadfully, Pārvatī became overwhelmed with fear and spontaneously and passionately threw herself into Śiva's lap, embracing him tightly.

Lord Śiva, experiencing the embrace characterized by the pressure of Pārvatī's high and full breasts, was instantly covered in horripilation. Filled with intense joy aroused by Smara (the god of love), he rejoiced greatly.

Thus satisfied by the various playful gestures and charms of Pārvatī, Lord Śiva, who wears the moon as his crest-jewel, continued to dwell on Mount Kailāsa and rejoiced in the company of his self-controlled attendants (Gaṇas).
Carrying the intense energy of Śiva, Agni reached Indra in the assembly where he was seated with the other gods.
Indra, the lord with a thousand eyes, looked at Agni, who had a loathsome appearance, was difficult to behold, and was surrounded by a dark smoky aura.
Upon seeing Agni in such a state, Indra’s mind became disturbed, and he pondered for a long time about the consequences arising from Śiva’s wrath.
While being observed moment after moment by the gods with perplexed faces, Agni sat down on the seat respectfully offered by Indra.
Indra asked, "O Agni, how did you come to this miserable state?" Thus questioned, Agni sighed and began to speak.
"O leader of the gods, because your command cannot be transgressed, I assumed the form of a pigeon, trembling with extreme fear."
I approached Lord Śiva while he was united with Gauri. I encountered the terrifying form of Śiva, the enemy of Cupid, who appeared like Death himself.
O Indra, seeing me as a disguised bird, the wise Śiva recognized me and, in his anger, intended to sacrifice me into the blazing fire of his third eye.
When I praised him with sweet, meaningful words and a humble posture, the Lord became pleased; for whom is praise not a source of satisfaction?
Lord Śiva, the refuge and savior of all, saved me from being devoured by his irresistible, blazing fire of anger and from my intense fear.
Śiva, abandoning the intense desire for the embrace of Himālaya's daughter Parvatī, ceased his activity out of shame arising from the excessive passion of their amorous play.

That unfailing semen, which was extremely hard to carry and capable of incinerating the three worlds, having fallen due to the interruption of their union, was instantly placed upon Agni's body by Śiva.
Agni addresses Indra, stating that he is unable to carry his own scorched and heavy body, which has been burnt by that unbearable, fiery energy of Śiva.
Agni cries out to Indra (Vāsava), asking him to be ready to save his life, as he is being consumed by the exceedingly great and fierce luster of Śiva.
Having heard Agni's words, Indra, the lord of the gods, contemplated in his mind a means to alleviate Agni's intense suffering.
Indra, the Lord of Heaven, touching Agni’s limbs that were scorched by Śiva’s energy with his hand, spoke these words to the Fire-god.
Indra praises Agni, saying that he himself satisfies the gods, ancestors, and humans through the ritual offerings of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Hantakāra, because he is their sole mouth.
When priests offer oblations into Agni, they are purified of their sins and enjoy heaven; thus, Agni is indeed the primary cause for the attainment of heaven.
O Agni! Ascetics who offer oblations purified by mantras into you attain the perfection of their penance, for you are the lord and master of all austerities.
You deliver the oblations to the Sun, who then rains as a cloud. From rain comes food, and from food come all beings. Thus, you are effectively the father of the entire world.

Addressing Agni, Indra states that Agni moves within all living beings as the internal digestive fire. All beings originate from him, and consequently, he is the personification of life itself and the bestower of vital breath to the entire universe.
You are the sole benefactor of this entire world. In the matter of accomplishing this specific divine task, who else besides you has the capability or courage to venture forward?

O Agni, you alone are capable of fulfilling the objective of these hosts of gods. For one like you, whose life-vow is to perform praiseworthy service for others, even facing destruction or adversity in the process is honorable.
Goddess Gaṅgā has already been propitiated by us with devotion. When you immerse yourself in her waters, she will cool the intense heat generated within you by Śiva's seed.
O Agni, go to the River Gaṅgā at once and do not delay. In tasks that are mandatory and urgent, prompt action is the key to achieving success.
The Goddess Gaṅgā is herself the watery manifestation of Lord Śiva. Therefore, she will be able to receive and bear that unbearable seed of the enemy of Smara (Śiva) from you.
After saying this, Indra became silent. Agni, having been dismissed and taking leave of Indra, set out towards the celestial river Gaṅgā.
Agni, having traveled the distance, reached the Goddess Gaṅgā, the celestial river who destroys every bit of suffering and distress.
She is the ladder for ascending to heaven and the presiding deity of the path to spiritual liberation. She removes the heavy accumulation of sins and enables one to cross over all difficulties.
Dwelling in the matted locks of Lord Śiva, she is the destroyer of sins. She grants liberation even to those bound by worldly attachments and serves as the eternal upholder of Dharma.
The river Gaṅgā, who originated from the water of Viṣṇu's feet and descended from the world of Brahmā, purifies the three worlds tirelessly with her three streams.
As if wearing a gracious expression, Gaṅgā invited the approaching Agni with her uplifted wave-like hands for the successful fulfillment of the intended purpose.
Accompanied by intoxicated swans warbling sweetly, Gaṅgā addressed Agni, saying, 'I bestow blessings and destroy sorrows.'
The celestial river Gaṅgā approached Agni as if she were pleased, with her rising waves rushing towards the nearby bank.
Then Agni, afflicted by heat and having reached the river, immersed himself in her. Do those overpowered by calamity ever endeavor to delay their relief?
Immersed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, which brings welfare, removes fatigue, bears merit, and grants liberation, Agni attained great peace.
In the high-waved Gaṅgā, the divine seed of Lord Śiva, which was carried by Agni, was transferred into the river that absorbs the calamity of internal heat.
When that seed of Śiva was received by the river, Agni emerged from her waters feeling great relief and happiness.
Agni, as if bathed in showers of nectar by the waters of Gaṅgā, felt supreme satisfaction and departed the way he had come.
The celestial river Gaṅgā, upon receiving the mighty and unbearable seed of Lord Śiva, the conqueror of Love, began to experience intense heat and suffering.
Distressed and feeling as if scorched by hundreds of flames from the world-destroying fire at the end of an aeon, the aquatic creatures abandoned the hot waters of the river and emerged outside.
That river bore the violent, rising, and unbearable waters, which were heated by that fierce and terrible energy of the seed of Śiva.
In the month of Māgha, when the Sun—the eye of the world—was just about to rise, the six Kṛttikās went to the celestial river Gaṅgā to take their ritual bath.

With hundreds of white waves touching the clouds, the river seemed to be recounting the various acts of the residents of heaven, such as beholding her, bathing in her, and performing ritual sipping of her waters.
The river's banks were profusely strewn with heaps of flowers, Dūrvā grass, and sacred rice grains, all suitable for the ritual offerings performed by the great sages after their baths.
The river was occupied by sages who were absorbed in meditation on Brahman and Yoga, seated in the Brahmāsana posture, some in Yogic sleep, and others using Yogic binding straps for support.
The river was frequented by divine sages who stood on the tips of their big toes with their gaze fixed on the Sun, chanting hymns to the Supreme Brahman.
Then, seeing the divine river goddess, the Kṛttikās rejoiced. Indeed, whom does this river, flowing with nectar, not delight once she is seen?
The Kṛttikās felt great devotion in their hearts for the river whom Lord Śiva, the moon-crested one, carries on his head and whose mere sight is known to be meritorious.
With their sins washed away and bowing their heads deeply, the Kṛttikās saluted the divine goddess Gaṅgā, who sprang from the foot of Viṣṇu and who points the way to the state of liberation.
The Kṛttikās, filled with faith and devotion, praised the celestial river Gaṅgā, who is a surety for liberation and easily reached only through great fortunes.
Endowed with penance, the Kṛttikās bathed in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā, which act as a messenger for union with liberation, thereby washing away all their taints.
After bathing in the river, which was accessible to them due to their fully ripened good fortune, the Kṛttikās joyfully considered their lives to have achieved their ultimate purpose.
Immediately after their immersion in the Gaṅgā, the unfailing seed of Śiva entered the bodies of the Kṛttikās.
Bearing that fierce and fiery power of Śiva, which was extremely difficult to sustain, the Kṛttikās experienced intense heat as if they were submerged in an ocean of poison.
Unable to carry that unbearable burden, the distressed Kṛttikās emerged from the water appearing as if they were carrying a blazing fire within them.
The great, shining, and unfailing seed of Śiva, which had been cast off by the river, entered the wombs of the Kṛttikās and attained the state of an embryo.
The wise Kṛttikās, realizing they were pregnant and unable to bear it, were immediately seized by deep despair due to shame and fear of their husbands.
Then, overcome by fear and shame, they abandoned the fetus in a forest of reeds (Śaravaṇa) and returned to their respective homes.

The abandoned seed, tender like a moon-digit, manifested as a child with six faces. These faces radiated measureless splendor, rivaling hundreds of suns and reaching toward the sky, as if competing with the greatness of Lord Śiva himself.

The personified celestial river Gaṅgā, being entreated by all the gods headed by Indra who approached her with humility, quickly offered her breast, which was overflowing with nectar, to the child and made him drink from it.

Drinking the flood of nectar from Gaṅgā's breasts and growing rapidly moment by moment, the child, being attended to by the six Kṛttikās who had arrived there, attained a marvelous and indescribable form.
A very intense dispute arose among Gaṅgā, Agni, and the Kṛttikās—all of whom had eyes filled with tears of joy—as each wished to take possession of that divine child.
Meanwhile, Lord Śiva, traversing the sky in a celestial chariot with the daughter of the Mountain King (Pārvatī) for a pleasure trip, arrived at that spot with a speed surpassing that of the mind.
Driven by natural parental love, Pārvatī and Śiva—their hearts filled with immense joy and their eyes overflowing with tears—beheld the six-faced child, who was only six days old.

Then the Goddess Pārvatī asked Śiva, "Who is this child with a divine form standing before us? Who is the most fortunate man who is his father, and who is the foremost among blessed women who is his mother?"
"Are these the celestial Gaṅgā, Agni, and the six Kṛttikās? They are quarreling, each claiming 'He is my son, not yours,' and are displaying a false sense of confusion and embarrassment."

"O Lord, whose offspring is this, serving as an ornament to all the three worlds? Does he belong to one of these present here, or to someone else among the gods, demons, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Nagas, or Rakshasas?"
Having heard these words from his curious beloved, Lord Śiva, adorned with a pure smile, spoke words that were destined to cause intense joy and happiness.

"O auspicious one! This hero, the delighter of the three worlds, is indeed your own son—you, the mother of a great hero. How could such a creation, a benefactor to the gods, belong to any woman other than you?"

Lord Śiva addresses Pārvatī, stating that she alone is the primary cause for the creation of this child for the welfare of the world. He asks her to consider this truth, noting that it is only fitting for a jewel to be found in the ocean.

Śiva asks Pārvatī to listen attentively to the sequence of events. He explains that the seed he placed in Agni was transferred into the river Gaṅgā, and subsequently reached the Kṛttikās when they went for a bath.

That unfailing seed attained the form of a fetus and was placed by the Kṛttikās in a clump of reeds. At that spot, an unprecedented great celebration took place involving all living and non-living beings of the entire universe.

Addressing Pārvatī as the daughter of Himavat, Śiva tells her that because of this son, who is beautiful to the entire world, she has become the foremost among mothers of virtuous sons. He urges her to stop delaying and take her son onto her lap.
When Lord Śiva finished speaking, Pārvatī, the mother of the entire universe, was immediately filled with intense joy. Her body thrilled with emotion, and she prepared to act with great haste.
Being saluted by the celestial beings who stood in the sky with folded hands touching their crowns, Pārvatī descended from the chariot. Her mind was filled with intense longing to embrace her son.

Eagerly, she approached her son, ignoring the Gaṅgā, Agni, and the Kṛttikās who were bowing to her with folded hands. Truly, what mother would not be intoxicated with joy during the celebration of her son's birth?

With her eyes clouded by tears of joy, she could not see him for a moment even though he was right in front of her. However, as she touched him with her bud-like hand, she experienced an indescribable and unprecedented state of supreme happiness.
The infant finally came into the range of vision of the Goddess, whose eyes were wide with wonder and joy, overflowing with tears, and brimming with an intensified sentiment of maternal affection.

Gazing at him, she momentarily desired a thousand eyes to look at him without blinking. Indeed, whose mind would ever feel fully satisfied at any moment while performing the auspicious act of gazing upon one's own son?

Gaurī, having taken the child with her lotus-like hands—which usually rest on the backs of the bowed gods and demons—placed him on her lap. The child, newly born, appeared as beautiful as the full moon on a pūrṇimā night.
The moon-faced Pārvatī, placing her son—who was like a storehouse of nectar and the unique hero of the world—upon her lap, became the most venerable among all mothers.
The mother of the universe, moistened by natural maternal love and filled with an intense flood of joy, began to lactate for her only son who was resting on her lap.

The son of the six mothers (Kārttikeya) drank the nectar-like milk of Pārvatī, the mother of all three worlds, while being watched longingly and repeatedly by the Kṛttikās on the banks of the celestial river.

The wife of Lord Śiva, her face brimming with tears of happiness, kissed the six faces of her son one after another with her single lotus-face, which looked like the beauty of multiple lotuses blooming from one stem.
Pārvatī, holding her son, shone brilliantly like a golden creeper of the Himālayas bearing fruit, like the celestial Gaṅgā with a blooming lotus, or like the eastern sky holding the newly risen moon.
With a delighted mind, supported by the hand offered carefully by the moon-crested Śiva, Pārvatī ascended the sky-scraping celestial chariot while holding Kumāra on her lap.

Lord Maheśvara, with his hair standing on end due to joy, took the child from Pārvatī’s lap. Out of mutual affection for their son, she then took the child back from his lap, and this cycle continued.
Lord Śiva, being embraced by Pārvatī who was holding their pure son—a feast of nectar for the eyes—departed from the residence at the high speed of the celestial chariot.

Then Lord Śambhu, having reached his exceedingly beautiful abode on the high crystal peak of Mount Kailāsa, commanded the vast hosts of Ganas and the leaders of the Pramathas to prepare for a grand festival.
Then, the entire host of Śiva's attendants, filled with immense joy and being well-prepared, gathered to celebrate the festival of the birth of the son of Pārvatī.
The attendants erected excellent golden arches on the crystal palaces; these arches were adorned with celestial blossoms and their brilliance lit up the sky.
Then, a powerful and deep-sounding kettledrum, beaten by others, resounded across all directions to announce the great festival, just as if the gods were celebrating in the mortal world.
In the house of Pārvatī, during the festival, auspicious songs were sung by the beautiful Gandharva and Vidyādhara women who had gathered there and were being honored.
The Divine Mothers approached the son of Pārvatī like mothers, holding auspicious gifts. Having placed Dūrvā grass and grains on his head as a blessing, they took him onto their laps.
As the musical instruments and drums sounded deeply, the Apsarasas danced with passion. Their dance was perfectly synchronized, following the song's rhythm and permeated with artistic emotions.
Pleasant winds blew, the directions became clear, the sacrificial fire burned brightly without smoke, waters became pure, and the sky instantly turned serene during that festival.
The kettledrums in the palace sounded loudly, mingling with the deep blast of conchs. In the sky, the celestial chariots of the gods moved along, showering heaps of flowers.
In this manner, the birth festival of the son of Śiva and Pārvatī filled the entire universe of moving and unmoving beings with joy; only the fortune of the demon Tāraka trembled in fear.
Then the young Kumāra won the hearts of Śiva and Pārvatī with his various charming childhood pranks, which were sources of great joy. Indeed, are not the playings of a child always delightful?
Out of great joy and with eagerness, Lord Maheśvara and Pārvatī kissed the beautiful, toothless faces of their son, Kārttikeya, one by one with their single faces.
The young boy Kārttikeya increased the joy of his parents through his playful attempts at walking, sometimes stumbling, sometimes steady, sometimes trembling, and at other times firm.

His moon-like face brightened by causeless smiles and his body grey with the dust of the courtyard, the child Kārttikeya, sitting on the laps of his parents and speaking unintelligible words, increased their happiness.
Grabbing the horns of Śiva's bull, playfully touching Pārvatī's lion, and pulling the thin tip of Bhṛṅgin's top-knot, the child became a source of great delight to his parents.

Sitting on Śiva's lap and opening his own mouths, the child counted the teeth of the serpent around Śiva's neck as 'one, nine, two, ten, five, seven'. Thus, his charming childish innocence was displayed.
Inserting his finger into the hollow mouths of the skulls in the garland around Śiva's neck, Prince Kārttikeya eagerly tried to pull out the teeth, mistaking them for pearls.
After diving deep into the cold waves of the Gaṅgā on Śiva's head, Kārttikeya warmed his lotus-like hands, which had become numb with cold, in the fire of Śiva's third eye.
As Śiva bent his neck and his matted hair bowed forward, the crescent moon on his crown hung down. The child, with great curiosity, kissed that moon sweetly for a long time.
In this manner, captivated by the pleasing childhood plays of their son and entirely absorbed in that joy, Pārvatī and Śiva did not even notice the passing of day and night.
Performing various charming and blissful childhood activities, the Lord Kārttikeya attained supreme intellect and fresh youth on the sixth day itself, by which he mastered all scriptures and weapons.

Then Indra, the beloved of Śacī, whose mind was distressed by the harassment caused by cruel demons, approached Lord Śiva (the enemy of Andhaka) accompanied by all the gods, just as a thirsty bird approaches a rain-bearing cloud.

Indra somehow descended from the celestial path through the clouds—a path he had rendered unused out of fear of his arrogant enemies—toward the mountain Kailāsa, which was sanctified by the footprints of Lord Śiva and Goddess Pārvatī.

Then Indra, leaning on the hand of his charioteer Mātali, descended from his chariot and proceeded toward the abode of Lord Śiva, who is of the nature of a cloud. He resembled a person parched by thirst in summer moving toward water.
As he walked, Indra saw his single self reflected many times in the crystal ground of the mountain. Observing himself thus multiplied, he reached the residence of the Lord Śiva.
He reached the gate of the palace courtyard of Lord Śiva, which was guarded by the fierce Nandin. Nandin held a golden staff adorned with an array of various sparkling gems.
Then Nandin, placing his golden staff under his arm, approached Indra and immediately welcomed him with great respect. Afterward, he went in person and announced Indra's arrival to Lord Śiva.
Having received a command from Lord Śiva through a mere movement of his eyebrow, Nandin led the way and escorted Indra, along with the other gods, into the assembly hall of the Lord of the Universe.
The thousand-eyed Indra beheld Lord Śiva in a gem-studded assembly hall. The Lord was surrounded by numerous venerable Gaṇas of various forms, led by prominent figures such as Caṇḍī and Bhṛṅgin.

He saw Śiva wearing matted hair tied up high, which was brilliant with the glistening rays of gems from the heads of serpents. His hair attained a likeness to the lofty peak of Mount Sumeru, which is rich with glowing minerals.

He saw the Lord bearing the river Ganges, which was flowing over his matted hair with high waves. The Ganges, with her foam as white as autumn clouds, seemed to be laughing at Goddess Pārvatī, who was seated on the Lord’s lap.

Lord Śiva is described bearing the moon on his head. Due to the reflections in the waves of the Gaṅgā, the single moon appears to have become manifold. The moon, white as frost, shines with clusters of moving rays, illuminating the Lord's head as he carries it.

Śiva possesses a third eye on his forehead with increasing radiance that surpasses the brilliance of his other two eyes (the sun and moon). This eye, which consumed Kāmadeva, glows like the cataclysmic fire that appears at the end of a Yuga.

Lord Śiva appears as if being worshipped or attended by the sun and the moon themselves, who have taken the form of his two magnificent earrings. These earrings are adorned with precious gems and cast a wide halo of brilliant light from his ears.
The Lord shines beautifully due to the great radiating luster of his blue throat. It appears as if Gaurī, out of playful curiosity, has tied a necklace made of blue sapphires around his neck.

Lord Śiva's body is smeared white with the funeral ashes of gods and demons destroyed by Time. Wearing the hide of a great elephant, he possesses the majestic beauty of the snowy Himālaya mountains capped by rising clouds.

Wielding his trident high—the weapon that ends all battles—Śiva holds a skull-bowl in his hand. He is adorned with ornaments of human bone fragments, a sight so formidable that even Viṣṇu attempts to avert it.

On his neck, Śiva wears an ancient garland of skulls. These skulls have regained consciousness and are breathing again, even chanting the Vedas, because they are constantly bathed in the overflowing nectar raining down from the moon on Śiva's crown.

Lord Śiva shines while Pārvatī sits gracefully on his lap. With her complexion like a fresh golden creeper, she resembles a flash of lightning illuminating a white autumnal cloud, which is represented by the ash-smeared Lord.

With his hand, Śiva grasps the Pināka bow, which cannot be wielded by anyone else. This is the same Lord who playfully burnt Kāmadeva in the past, slew the arrogant demon Andhaka, and brought widowhood to the wives of the great demons.

Lord Śiva is seated upon an auspicious throne that features a golden footstool and is beautifully inlaid with precious rubies. He is being fanned by two of his attendants using fly-whisks as white as the rays of the moon.

While Kumāra was intently practiced in the science of arms, the amazed Gaṇas approached and gazed at him. As the crystal mountain Kailāsa seemed to perform a lustration ritual for him with its radiance, Śiva cast his joyful eyes upon his son.

Upon seeing the Lord of Pārvatī in such a majestic state, Indra, the husband of Śacī, became momentarily overwhelmed with emotion. Indeed, whose mind would not be stirred when standing before the most brilliant and supreme radiance?

Indra, beholding Śiva with his thousand eyes that resembled a forest of blooming lotuses, shone brilliantly. With his hair standing on end due to devotion, he looked like a mango tree covered in clusters of blossoms.

Having beheld Lord Śiva with his thousand eyes, Indra felt immensely fulfilled. However, he then reflected upon those many eyes covering his body, which usually caused his wife Śacī's anger, and for a moment considered them a deformity.
Then Indra, seeing Kumāra standing near Maheśvara, equipped with weapons and possessing the strength of Mount Meru, finally felt a firm hope in his heart for victory over his enemy.

Nandi addressed Śiva: 'O illustrious Blue-throated Lord, the King of Heaven stands before you, seeking an opportunity to prostrate. O Three-eyed Lord, please look upon this thousand-eyed Indra with a favorable and gracious gaze.'
Thus, with folded hands, Nandi approached and placed his golden staff under his arm. Seeking to remain a recipient of Śiva's grace, he then spoke these words to the enemy of Smara (Śiva).

Then the enemy of Tripura, who is served by all three worlds, cast a gracious glance upon Indra, who is served by the gods. That affectionate look of Śiva was like a refreshing shower of nectar upon the King of Heaven.

Indra, the foremost among the inhabitants of heaven, bowed his head before Śiva, the supreme Lord of the universe. As he bowed, a shower of Pārijāta flowers fell from the tip of his crown onto the feet of the God of gods.
By bowing with deep devotion to Maheśvara, who is the sole object of worship for all worlds, Indra, the King of the gods, became a supreme and pure vessel of total spiritual fulfillment.

Thereafter, the hosts of gods, filled with deep devotion, bowed down in succession before Śiva (the enemy of Pura) in front of His divine attendants, touching the ground near His footstool with their deeply inclined heads.
Indra, directed by Lord Śiva, sat down on an auspicious golden seat brought by the attendants and experienced great joy. Indeed, who does not feel delighted by the favor shown by the Lord?
The other gods were also honored by the Lord in turn with a smiling glance. Attaining a sense of special satisfaction, all the deities sat down within His range of vision.

Then, the Lord, His heart melting with compassion, observed the groups of gods headed by Indra. Seeing them with folded hands, their glory vanished and their faces showing exhaustion, He spoke to them.
O dwellers of heaven! Alas, why do the faces of you, who possess infinite prowess and the best of heroic weapons, bear the wretchedness of a lotus withered by drops of frost?
O inhabitants of heaven! Have you been displaced from heaven despite your vast store of merit? You still bear the long-carried marks of your own sovereignty, yet you seem to have lost your status.
O gods! Why do you, who are great and possessed of self-respect, wander on the earth like ordinary humans, having abandoned your divine abode?
Why has that divine abode, which is extraordinarily beautiful, exalted, and uniquely attained, suddenly departed from you, just as long-accumulated merit leaves one due to some sinful lapse?
O noble gods! Why has your unshakeable fortitude left your hearts, much like water disappears from a deep lake due to the intense heat of summer?
O gods! All of you, led by Indra, appear equally distressed. Tell me, what harm has been done to you by the great demon Tāraka, the conqueror of the three worlds?

Lord Śiva declares that he alone is capable of thwarting the defeat caused by that great demon Tāraka. He uses a metaphor, asking who else besides a massive rain-cloud can remove the calamity of a forest fire that scorches the woods.
When Lord Śiva, the destroyer of Kāmadeva, spoke these words, the gods led by Indra quickly took heart. Their faces, rippling with tears of intense joy, regained their natural splendor and grace.
