Then, as Śiva finished speaking and an opportunity arose, Indra spoke. He noted that words uttered at the right moment certainly lead to a great and successful outcome.

Indra addresses Śiva as the All-knowing One, stating that through the eternal lamp of his knowledge—which dispels the darkness of ignorance and possesses unfailing light—everything in the past, present, and future is visible to him.

Indra asks Śiva if he is not aware that they have been expelled from heaven by Tāraka. He describes the demon as a devourer of gods who attained lordship through the unbearable strength and unstoppable effort of his arms.

Having obtained an unfailing boon from Brahmā, Tāraka became instantly intent on conquering the three worlds. Fierce with his powerful arms, he now considers all the gods, including the Sun-god, as insignificant as a blade of grass.

Indra recalls that when they worshipped Brahmā with praises in the past, he prophesied that the son of Lord Śiva (the enemy of Kāmadeva) would become their commander-in-chief and slay this demon in battle.
Indra laments that from that time until today, the gods have been forced to endure the unbearable pain of defeat. They have suffered his commands like a painful thorn lodged deep within their hearts.

Indra requests Śiva to personally appoint his son as their commander. He likens this act to a fresh rain-cloud appearing for plants withered by the scorching summer sun, bringing them relief and great joy.

Indra emphasizes that Śiva's son, by leading them in battle, will uproot that great demon who is like a thorn in the heart of the three worlds' prosperity. By doing so, he will finally bring about the complete removal of the gods' sorrows.

Indra prays to Śiva, saying that in the great battle, let the ten directions resound with the wailing of the wives of the great demons whose necks will be severed by the sharp weapons of Śiva's son, Kārttikeya.

Indra continues, expressing hope that when the demon Tāraka is sacrificed like an animal on the battlefield by Śiva's son, the inhabitants of heaven may finally untie the braids of the beautiful captive women, signaling their liberation.
As Indra spoke thus, Śiva (the lord of beings), whose anger was provoked by the wicked deeds of the demons but who felt compassion for the gods, spoke once again.
Śiva addressed the gods, led by Indra, asking them to listen to his words. He stated that he is ready for the task and is acting through his son and others for their benefit.
Śiva explains that although he is self-controlled, he accepted Pārvatī only for this reason: that the heroic son born of her would be the one to slay this enemy (Tāraka).
Śiva suggests that it is appropriate for the gods to appoint Kumāra as the commander of the army to destroy the enemy, so that Indra may once again rule over heaven along with the other deities.
Having said this, Lord Śiva spoke to his son Kumāra, who was eager for the great 'festival' of the terrible battle, saying, "O son, slay the enemy of the gods in battle."
Kumāra accepted Śiva's command with a bowed head; indeed, for those devoted to their father, following his command is the highest duty.
When Śiva spoke thus regarding the war with the demons, Pārvatī rejoiced in the prowess of her son. Indeed, what mother of a hero would not feel joy in her son's valor?

Indra, the leader of the gods, became exceedingly joyful upon receiving Kumāra—the mighty son of Śiva who gives fearlessness to the world and causes the wives of demons to weep. Truly, who would not be intoxicated with joy when their heart's desire is fulfilled?
Dressed in magnificent attire befitting his departure and followed by hosts of gods, Kumāra then bowed his head and prostrated at the feet of Lord Śiva, the sovereign of the three worlds.

Blessing him with the words, "O brave child, slay the enemy of Indra in battle and bring stability to the throne of the king of gods," Lord Śiva joyfully smelled Kumāra's head as he bowed and hailed him.
Bending low with a most humble head, he paid obeisance to his mother Pārvatī's feet. The torrent of joyful tears shed by her became the ceremonial consecration for him, the greatest of heroes.
Placing him on her lap and embracing him tightly, the affectionate daughter of the Himālayas kissed his head and said, "Conquer the enemy and make me, the mother of a hero, feel fulfilled."
Kumāra, the destined cause of the arrogant demon king's downfall and whose heart was eager for the festive fray of battle, devotedly took leave of Pārvatī and Śiva and set out towards the heavens.
Then the other gods also, having prostrated before Lord Maheśa and Goddess Pārvatī and having circumambulated them, all followed Kumāra, led by Indra.
As all the gods moved along with their radiant auras of throbbing light, the sky shone as if it were scattered all over by fierce clusters of stars even during the day.
In the midst of those moving gods, Kumāra, possessing superior loveliness and luster, shone like the Moon in the company of clusters of constellations, stars, and planets in the vast sky.
Accompanied by the son of Śiva and Pārvatī, Indra and the other gods crossed the celestial path of stars in just a moment and reached their own realm.
All the gods, having been so long subjected to the terror of the great demon, did not dare to enter their heavenly home immediately upon seeing it after such a long time; they hesitated for a moment.

Terrified of the impending battle, the gods began to quarrel among themselves at that very moment. Ironically, instead of fighting the enemy, they argued about who should go first to enter heaven (fleeing the battlefield), each urging the other to take the lead in their retreat.

With a desire to see their heavenly home again and with joyful yet trembling eyes, the gods fixed their gaze upon the lotus-face of Kumāra. Their eyes, though bright with hope, still betrayed the lingering anxiety and fear caused by their enemy, Tārakāsura.
Then, Kumāra, a true hero in battle, stood before them with a playful smile illuminating his moon-like face. Anticipating the imminent downfall of the demon Tāraka, he addressed the gathered gods.

Kumāra reassures the gods, telling them to abandon their fear and return to heaven immediately. He declares that the great demon, their long-time foe whom they have encountered before, should now face him and come within the range of his sight.

Kumāra vows that his arrows will swiftly make a sport of drinking the blood of that demon, whose arms move fiercely to humiliate the Goddess of Heaven by dragging her by the hair. He promises to end the demon's arrogance right here.

May my spear, which possesses unimpeded speed, immense power, and brilliant radiance, grant you joy by severing the head of the enemy who has brought such calamity upon the Goddess of Heaven. Kumāra invokes his divine weapon to restore peace to the gods.

Upon hearing the words of Kumāra (the son of Śiva), who was eager for battle to slay the demon, the entire host of gods rejoiced. Their faces, once clouded with fear, now blossomed like lotuses with pure smiles of relief and hope.

Indra, overwhelmed with intense joy that caused his thousand eyes to blossom and his skin to tingle, performed a beautiful ritual. He waved his own upper garment around Kumāra, an affectionate act meant to ward off the evil eye and honor the young hero.

Then the ancient creator, Brahmā, his four faces radiant with grace and his eyes brimming with tears of joy, performed a wondrous act. He tenderly kissed the six-faced Kumāra on each of his six heads, showing his deep affection and divine blessing.

The multitudes of Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Siddhas praised Kumāra from all sides with joyful cries of "Well done! Well done!" They gladdened the son of Śiva by hailing him with the words, "O Hero, be victorious!", as they celebrated his courage.

The divine sages, led by Nārada, hailed Kārttikeya, who was destined to defeat the enemy. They performed a protective ritual (niruñchanam) for him using their golden upper garments and bark-robes as auspicious offerings.

Casting away their fear due to the support of the infinite power of the spear-wielding Kārttikeya, the gods ventured to go back to heaven, just as elephants return to the forest when led by a powerful leader of the herd.
Then, the gods followed closely behind Kārttikeya, who desired to slay the enemy of Indra (Tāraka), just as the Pramatha attendants follow Śiva when he desires to burn the triple cities (Tripura).
The gods reached the celestial river (Mandākinī), whose floods were colored reddish-yellow by the body-unguents washed off from the celestial damsels who were constantly enjoying water-sports in it.
The river was repeatedly flooding the basins of the trees growing on its banks with formidable waves, which were stirred up by the trunks of the quarter-elephants (dig-gajas) playing in its waters.
The banks of the river were covered with high, excellent platforms made by playful celestial maidens using golden sand that contained rubies within.

The river's water was turned yellowish all over by the fallen pollen of blooming golden lotuses. These lotuses were being sung over by bees greedy for their fragrance and were swaying due to the play of rows of golden swans.
The river was bringing joy to travelers through the reflections of celestial beauties in its waves. These beauties had approached and stood on the bank out of curiosity to ask questions.

Indra rejoiced instantly upon seeing the celestial river, which he had not seen for a long time. Then, walking ahead as a guide, he respectfully showed the river to Kārttikeya, the son of Pārvatī and Śiva.
Surrounded by all the gods, Kārttikeya beheld the celestial river in front of him, which he had never seen before. He was filled with wonder, and his eyes lit up with a smile at the sight.

Having reached there, the devoted Kumāra, with his folded hands touching the edge of his crown, bowed to the goddess who is praised by the hosts of gods. With a bowed head and a delighted heart, he offered his salutations.
The breeze from the river served Guha. This breeze set the rows of blooming lotuses dancing, its great waves met in embraces before him, and it removed the sweat from his cheeks.
Then, while entering the pleasure garden of Indra called Nandana located ahead, the son of Shiva observed the garden where groups of Shāla trees had been split, broken, and uprooted.

Reflecting on how this garden of Indra, the enemy of Bala, was devastated and robbed of its glory by the enemy of the gods, Kumāra's eyes turned red and his face became terrifying to behold with knitted brows due to anger.
Kumāra beheld the city of Amarāvatī, the incomparable essence of the universe, now with its pleasure gardens razed, its aerial paths obstructed, and its grand palaces in ruins.
Seeing the city in such a wretched state, robbed of its glory and oppressed by a powerful foe like a defenseless woman without a protector, Kumāra was deeply moved by compassion within his heart.
Angry at the evil deeds of the enemy of gods, yet undeterred and eager for battle, Kumāra entered the capital of Indra along with the gods, observing its pitiful state.

In that city, seeing the rows of crystal palaces with shattered interiors caused by the tusks of demons' elephants, and their windows covered with the shed skins of great snakes, he was immediately struck with grief.
He observed the lakes which once had carved golden lotuses but were now polluted by the ichor of the elephants of the quarters, deserted by golden swans, and containing cracked slabs of lapis lazuli.
Seeing the plight of the oblong ponds of the pleasure-houses, now overgrown with young grass due to the enemy's neglect, Kumāra felt a heavy burden of sorrow and bewilderment.

Preceded by Indra, the leader of the gods, Kārttikeya was led to Indra's personal palace named Vaijayanta. The palace featured golden walls scarred by the tusks of Indra's divine elephants and gem-studded windows adorned with fine silken nets.
Guided by Indra and followed by all the gods, Kārttikeya entered the palace using a staircase that glittered with the multifaceted rays of various precious stones.

He reached that palace which had natural wish-fulfilling trees as arches, was decorated with Pārijāta flower garlands, and where great divine sages performed auspicious rites, filling the interior with immense joy.
With folded hands, Kārttikeya circumambulated the great seer Kaśyapa, the progenitor of both gods and demons, and bowed down to his feet using his six heads.

In the same manner, the son of Pārvatī (Kārttikeya), becoming humble with devotion, bowed deeply to the feet of Aditi, the mother of the gods and wife of the sage Kaśyapa, whose feet are worthy of worship by the entire world.

Kaśyapa and Aditi, the mother of the gods, both blessed him with such a benediction by which he would become the conqueror of the fiercely powerful Tāraka, who sought to conquer many worlds, in battle.
He bowed at the feet of the noble goddesses who had gathered there with Aditi to see him. Those virtuous wives, in turn, greeted him again with heartfelt words of blessing.
Then, the son of Śiva (Kārttikeya) saluted Śacī, the daughter of Puloman and wife of Indra. She, in return, honored and welcomed him with her blessings.
Then those seven divine mothers, filled with intense joy and led by Aditi and Indra's wife, approached and gave their foremost blessings to the son of Śiva as he bowed before them with devotion.

Thereafter, all the gods headed by Indra, filled with great joy, assembled and formally consecrated Kārttikeya, whose heart was overflowing with waves of happiness, as the commander-in-chief of the divine army.

The entire world of gods became free from all sorrow and gained hope for victory over their enemies, having found the opportunity for battle. This occurred as the son of Śiva (Kārttikeya), possessed of infinite valor, attained the complete glory of the entire divine army.
The son of Śiva (Kārttikeya), eager for battle and desiring victory, quickly prepared himself along with the gods to forcibly slay the great demon named Tāraka, the enemy of the gods.

Then the wielder of the spear and bow, Kārttikeya, ascended his great chariot named Vijitvara, which was faster than the mind, difficult to restrain or endure, and the very vessel for the goddess of victory.
A beautiful golden parasol, which wards off the calamities of heaven's fortune, causes distress to the prosperity of the demons, and destroys enemies, was held over Kārttikeya by someone.
Being fanned by beautiful chowries as white as autumn moonlight, Kārttikeya, eager for battle, was praised with powerful hymns by Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas who preceded him.

Then Indra, wearing a dress suitable for the march and carrying his thunderbolt that once clipped the wings of mountains, mounted his elephant Airāvata, which looked like a crystal peak, and followed Kārttikeya.
Agni followed Kārttikeya, seated upon a ram as large as a mountain peak and haughty with pride. Blazing intensely with fury against the enemy, he held his glorious and extremely powerful weapon.

Then Yama, the wielder of the staff of justice, joyfully followed Kārttikeya. He rode a formidable buffalo whose fierce body resembled a sapphire mountain and whose horns seemed to pierce the great clouds.
Then Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, terrifying in his intense hatred for the demons and filled with great anger, mounted a prideful ghost and followed Kārttikeya to join the fierce battle.
Varuṇa, holding his irresistible noose and formidable in battle, followed the son of Śiva. He was mounted on a massive Makara that looked as terrifying as a newly rising dark rain-cloud.

Vāyu, the god of wind, eager for the sport of battle, mounted his massive deer—which possessed unimpeded speed and could leap across the sky in an instant—and quickly followed Kārttikeya, the son of Śiva.

Kubera, carrying his massive mace that thirsted for the blood of enemies, followed Kārttikeya. Kubera appeared eager to dive into the vast ocean of the upcoming great battle, just as the son of Śiva was preparing to depart.

Then the Rudras, who carry the Pināka bow and have their matted locks bound by great serpents, followed Kārttikeya for the battle. Armed with blazing tridents and mounted upon great bulls as large as the Himālaya mountains, they marched forward.

Other groups of gods also followed Kārttikeya, having equipped themselves for war. Eager for the intoxicating festival of battle, they sat upon their powerful mounts, their faces radiant and blooming like lotuses due to their immense joy.

The divine armies marched, crowded with tall golden flagstaffs and brilliant with waving, colorful umbrellas. They were formidable, echoing with the terrifying roar of heavy moving chariots and the fierce trumpeting of great elephants accompanied by the clanging of their bells.
Then that great army of the gods departed, following the son of Śiva. The circles of light from their flashing, diverse weapons illuminated the sky and the surrounding horizons as they moved forward.

Immediately, the entire circle of the horizons, the sky, and the earth became completely packed without any breathing space. This was caused by the immense clamor of the marching gods and the dense multitudes of large banners belonging to the great armies.

Deep and dense sounds were produced by the beaten kettledrums, echoing throughout the circle of the horizons and filling the entire sky. These sounds were so ominous that they became the cause of the trembling of the wealth and power of the demons (the enemies of the gods).

The sky resounded intensely with the echoes of kettledrums, which were as threatening as the roar of the ocean being churned. These sounds were so powerful they caused the wives of the demons to miscarry, and the sky appeared agitated, as if filled by the thick clouds of dust raised by the army.

The dust of the golden mountain Meru gradually ascended into the sky. It was crushed by chariots, struck by the hooves of horses, spread in all directions by the flapping ears of great elephants, shaken by the banners, and carried upward by the winds.

The dust from the golden soil of the mountain valleys, dug up by the hooves of excellent chariot horses, was carried to the ends of the horizons by the whistling winds. This vast cloud of gold dust assumed a beautiful, tossing motion as it filled the air.

Driven by the wind and spreading through the armies, the golden dust rose intensely in all directions—below, above, in front, behind, and all around. This shimmering veil of dust surpassed even the glorious radiance of the rising sun.

The dust raised by the army from the golden ground spread across the sky and the horizons. Reddish-brown, resembling the intense hues of an untimely twilight, this thick layer of golden dust appeared like a dense mass of rising clouds.

Seeing their own reflections repeatedly on the polished golden ground, the great elephants mistook them for rival elephants emerging from the netherworld. Filled with rage, they struck at the reflections before them with their powerful tusks.

The elephants of the divine army, stained reddish-yellow by vermilion dust and moving with soft sounds, could no longer see their own reflections on the clear golden mountain slopes because the very dust they raised obscured the polished surface.

Thus, the army of Indra, eager to engage in the great battle as if it were a sport in the ocean, descended rapidly from the golden mountain. Their thunderous clamor filled the mountain caves, causing them to vibrate with the sound.

The lions sleeping in the vast caves of Mount Meru did not wake from their deep sleep, despite the fierce creaking of the great army's chariots and the loud trumpeting of the lordly elephants adorned with swinging bells.

The deep, terrifying sounds of the kettledrums, amplified by echoes in the mountain caves, and the heavy rumbling of the chariot wheels did not disturb the lions. Their calm unperturbed state truly demonstrated their natural status as the kings of beasts.

The deafening roar of the celestial army, which seemed to split the very slopes of the mountain, only served to increase the pride of the lions. Confident in their own strength and majesty, they grew even more spirited upon hearing the clamor.

Terrified by the commotion of the divine army, the deer fled quickly to a great distance. In contrast, the lions emerged from their cave dwellings and stood their ground with complete fearlessness and disdain, unbothered by the approaching forces.
The excellent soldiers of the divine army, watched from afar by the joyful and curious citizens of Amarāvatī, reached and spread across the vast expanses at the base of the celestial mountain Meru.
The sky bore the illusion of a spontaneous city of Gandharvas, created by the yellow, black, red, and white mineral dust rising in abundance from the slopes of Mount Meru and scattering everywhere.

A colossal sound, born from the movement and friction of the army, filled the entire universe. It reached the very limits of the ears and acted like a catalyst, further increasing the roar of an already agitated ocean.
The sound of the kettle-drums was completely drowned out by the widespread, deep trumpeting of great elephants, the terrifying neighing of horses, and the dense, fierce creaking of the chariots.
In an instant, the dust raised by the celestial army settled everywhere—on the hair, eyes, eyelashes, and breasts of the demon-harem women, as well as on the banners, elephants, chariots, and horses.

Seeing the sky covered with dense army dust that obscured the sun, the swans mistook it for monsoon clouds and flew toward Lake Mānasa, while the peacocks began to dance joyfully under the same illusion.
The golden banners of the army, fluttering amidst the thick dust that resembled fresh dark clouds in the sky, shone brilliantly like flashes of lightning.
Seeing the vast space between heaven and earth completely choked with layers of dust, people wondered whether the dust was falling from the sky to the earth or rising from the earth to the sky.

The vision of all living beings was completely blocked in every direction—up, down, front, back, and side—by the dense heaps of army dust, which were so thick they seemed almost solid enough to be pierced by a needle.

The sky roared deeply and incessantly with the thunderous sounds of various musical instruments. These sounds were so powerful they surpassed the scent of rut from the world-elephants and were amplified by echoes within the celestial chariots.

The vast army marched across the earth, and being too large to fit anywhere, it spilled into the great sky. Despite being so crowded and distressed, did it not find itself fleeing in all directions, overwhelmed by its own immense size?

The entire world became as if breathless and agitated by the trumpeting of elephants dripping with ichor, the neighing of tall horses, and the thunderous sounds of the rims of moving chariots belonging to the army.
The quarters of the sky became excessively resonant, filled with the deep roars of great elephants, the tinkling of swinging bells, and the joyous shouts of brave warriors ready for battle.

Rivers were instantly filled by the waves of ichor flowing from lordly elephants. These streams, filled with dust and trodden by horses, turned into mud and were then flattened into dry land by the passing chariots.
Low-lying areas became dry land, and high areas were lowered. The ground, dug up by the hooves of galloping horses, was leveled on all sides by the weight of passing chariots and lordly elephants.

The world was thrown into total agitation by the beating of kettle-drums, which echoed terrifyingly in the sky and quarters, were powerful enough to split mountain slopes, and seemed to playfully churn the very oceans.

Lakhs of banners, their cloths flickering in the wind and blocking the view of the horizons, decorated with tinkling golden bells, were submerged in the massive ocean of dust that had risen into the sky.

The beating of the army's drums could no longer be heard, as they were completely drowned out by the fierce, constant ringing of bells and the terrifying roars of intoxicated elephants that filled the air.
Seeing the quarters of the sky filled with dust and echoing with the fierce noise of the army, the sun disappeared from view, enveloped on all sides by the dense darkness caused by the rising dust.

The quarters, personified as a woman, defiled by the dust and previously invaded by the impetuous soldiers, seemed to roar back deeply through the thick echoes of the kettle-drums, as if out of intense resentment.

A strange reversal seemed to occur: the elephants, looking like mountains moved by strong winds, filled the sky (due to the dust), while the heavy chariots, resembling massive clouds, covered the earth.

At the time of the great dissolution for the powerful demons, the divine armies surged, filling the entire space between the sky and the earth. Like boundless oceans with terrifying roars in which massive mountains sink, these celestial forces grew immense and overwhelming, signaling the impending destruction of their foes.

A heart-trembling rumor spread through the city of the demons that Indra, the enemy of the asuras, was approaching with his armies, having appointed the son of Śiva (Kārttikeya) as his commander-in-chief for the battle.

Upon hearing that the son of Śiva, the commander of the divine army accompanied by the goddess of victory, had arrived with the celestial forces, the great demons remained deeply agitated in their hearts for a long time.

Assembling in the city of the demon king, the messengers bowed with their folded hands touching their crowns and reported that Indra had arrived, accompanied by the son of Śiva, who was eager for battle.
Tārakāsura laughed mockingly, saying: 'How many times has Indra failed to conquer me, who has enslaved the three worlds? Does he now really think he will certainly win by the strength of Śiva's son?'

Then Tārakāsura, his lower lip trembling with rage and eager for the sport of conquering the three worlds, ordered his generals, who were arrogant in their physical might, to arm themselves for battle.
The commanders of the great armies immediately armed themselves and, with weapons raised high, stood at the magnificent gatehouse of the palace courtyard, which was crowded with submissive kings.
The king saw many army commanders presented by the gatekeeper; they had bowed to him, were seated on excellent mounts, and were fierce enough to churn the great ocean of battle.

Then the powerful Tāraka mounted his formidable chariot and set out; the chariot's sound drowned out the cries of the directional elephants, its path was unimpeded by mountains or seas, and it was capable of crushing Indra's forces.

The armies followed the marching king; they roared like the ocean at the world's end, their fluttering banners blocked the sunlight, and the massive dust they kicked up obscured the sun and the horizons.

As the great demon advanced toward the gods, the dust raised by his army settled on the elephants of the quarters; it blended with their white tusks, increasing their whiteness, but turned into mud on their temples wet with rut.

The great oceans, agitated by the deep sounds of the kettledrums of the armies which were fierce enough to split mountain caves, overflowed their shores. Simultaneously, the celestial river (Ganga) suddenly swelled up.
The celestial river, churned by the tumultuous sounds of Tāraka's vast army, washed the rows of heavenly palaces with its hundreds of high-rising waves and lotuses.
As the enemy of the gods (Tāraka) prepared to march, a series of inauspicious portents appeared before him, signaling his upcoming immersion in a bottomless ocean of sorrow.
A terrifying flock of ominous birds, eager for the feast of the soon-to-be-slain Daityas, flew in the unshaded sky directly above the demon army.
A violent wind arose, repeatedly breaking parasols and banners. It agitated the eyes of the soldiers with swirling dust and shook horses, elephants, and chariots, making it impossible to see.
Great serpents, dark as crushed collyrium and bearing terrifying forms, moved swiftly across the paths ahead, intensely vomiting poisonous fire from their mouths.
The Sun, the lord of days, assumed a frightful halo that looked like a circle of entwined terrifying serpents, as if to signal the impending bloodshed of the great demon out of intense enmity.
A pack of jackals gathered in front of the sun and howled harshly, as if eager to quickly and forcibly drink the blood of the demon king at the end of the battle.
Observing swift, flickering meteors falling all around the armies even during the day, people mentally anticipated a fatal calamity for the enemy of the gods.
A thunderbolt fell from the cloudless sky with a heart-rending, terrible roar, its blazing masses of light illuminating every corner of the heavens and the earth.

The sky rained down intensely with heaps of blazing charcoal along with blood and bones. Blazing jackals emitted smoke from their mouths, and the quarters were filled with dust as grey as a donkey's throat.

There arose a massive sound of an atmospheric explosion that shattered mountain peaks. This dense sound filled the hollows of the sky and the horizons, piercing the ears of all, resembling the terrifying roar of an enraged Kāla.

Due to a violent earthquake that agitated the oceans and split the mountains, the enemy's army was thrown into chaos; great elephants stumbled, horses fell, and soldiers clung to one another in terror.

In front of the enemy of the gods (Tārakāsura), all the dogs gathered, upturning their faces and fixing their gaze on the sun. They began to howl together with a pitiful, ear-piercing sound as they moved out.

Even though the demon Tāraka saw an intense series of ill-omens that promised terrible consequences, he, being bitten by misfortune, did not turn back from his resolve to march, driven by sheer anger.

Though the wise warned him of the dreadful consequences of these omens and tried to restrain him, the great demon still marched forward. Indeed, the beneficial advice of great souls goes in vain for one blinded by evil obstinacy.
His golden parasol, blown down to the ground by an adverse wind, looked like a large golden vessel laid out for the God of Death's feast to break his fast.
As if sensing the impending beheading of the demon, his crown seemed to weep excessively out of grief, with trembling pearls falling repeatedly like teardrops.
Agitated vultures, foretelling his certain death, repeatedly descended upon his head from all sides; though the followers tried to ward them off, the birds seemed determined to seize him.

On Tāraka's banner, the people saw a massive serpent. It possessed the deep dark luster of freshly cut collyrium, with jewels on its hoods emitting a circle of blazing rays, and its hissing breath carrying the fire of lethal poison.

A fierce fire suddenly broke out in the vicinity of the large chariot's horses. It consumed the decorative whisks on the horses' ears and manes, as well as the bows, arrows, and quivers belonging to the demon.

Even though the demon was repeatedly warned by such ill-omens indicating misfortune, he did not turn back due to being blinded by pride. At that moment, a divine voice of the gods echoed from the sky.
O pride-blinded one! Do not enter into battle out of arrogance for your own strength with Kārttikeya, who is accompanied by Indra and other victorious gods from all sides.
Just as the sun cannot be faced by the darkness of night, Guha, though only six days old, cannot be withstood face-to-face in battle by demons. How then can you hope to be his adversary?
He who created a cleft in Mount Krauñca with a single arrow—a mountain whose hundreds of cloud-touching peaks blocked the horizons—how can there be any comparison between a battle with him and you?
This refers to Paraśurāma, who, having learned archery from Śiva, extinguished the fire of his anger by performing an ablution with the thick blood of kings twenty-one times in battle.

Even Paraśurāma, the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, does not boast of battle before Kārttikeya. When such a great warrior of the three worlds is his opponent, what scope is there for you to persist in this war?
O deluded one! Abandon your pride quickly. Do not come within the range of Kārttikeya's powerful spear. Seek refuge in him, the world's great hero, so that you may live for a long time.
Hearing this weighty voice from the sky, the ego-driven great demon, who normally made all three worlds tremble, himself trembled with rage. He then looked up and spoke loudly to the sky.
"O sky-dwellers, partisans of Kārttikeya! What are you saying? Have you already forgotten the agony of the wounds inflicted by my arrows?"

The jackals positioned in the sky wailed freely with harsh cries at the edge of the forest, like intoxicated dogs in the nights of the month of Kārttika, as if mocking or threatening the infant who was born only six days ago.

The demon Tāraka declares that due to association with the gods, the pitiable child Kārttikeya will surely meet his end, just as an innocent man dies when associated with thieves. Therefore, he decides to kill the gods first and then the child.
As the great demon Tāraka spoke these terrifying words and wielded his massive sword in great anger, the gods, their knees trembling and knocking against each other in fear, fled far away.
Then, laughing monstrously out of pride, the chariot-warrior Tāraka drew his excellent sword from its scabbard and commanded his charioteer, "Take the chariot quickly to Indra's presence!"
Moving forward in his chariot driven by the charioteer at a speed faster than thought, the great demon then reached the boundless and terrifying ocean of the celestial army that lay before him.
Seeing the vast army of the gods before him, that hero Tāraka, who was eager for the sport of battle, experienced an abundant thrill of joy upon his two fierce, staff-like arms.

Then the scouts and soldiers of Mahendra's army, faster than the mind and filled with great impetuosity for the deadly play of battle, rushed forward, questioning why those eager for combat were delaying the fight.
The soldiers of Indra approached the ocean-like army of the demon-foe standing before them; raising their arms, they loudly announced their names to the enemies on all sides.

The great demons became highly agitated upon seeing the vast ocean of the Daitya army approaching. However, all those warriors in the battle were easily contained within a single corner of the eye of Kārttikeya, the son of Śiva.

Kārttikeya, the son of Śiva, looked upon the armies of the gods—who were terrified by the enemy forces—with an eye showering the nectar of grace, viewing the impending great battle as a festive occasion.

Upon seeing Śaktidhara (Kārttikeya), the gods led by Indra felt encouraged in the battle. They rejoiced at the prospect of conquering their enemies. Indeed, the association with an excellent leader inspires valor in everyone.

Both the soldiers of Indra and their enemies, desiring victory, rushed toward each other in battle with weapons raised. Their names and heroic deeds were loudly proclaimed by bards as they engaged in combat.

As the two vast oceans of the divine and demonic armies collided like the end of the world, overstepping all bounds and pervading every direction, a massive, angry roar arose. This intense tumult, serving as a guest to Death, was powerful enough to shatter mountain cliffs and fill the entire expanse of the universe.
Then a fierce and great battle commenced between the armies of Indra and the demons. The conflict was characterized by terrifying volleys of missiles and weapons launched mutually by both sides.

The battle was fought between equals: foot soldiers charged at foot soldiers, charioteers engaged charioteers for combat, cavalrymen attacked cavalrymen, and those mounted on elephants sought out opponents similarly mounted on elephants.
As the brave warriors rushed toward each other steadily for combat, the chief bards of their respective lineages clearly proclaimed their names and titles to announce their presence on the field.
The great heroes, though eager for battle, paused for a moment and turned their attention toward the groups of bards who were reciting the long lists of their past heroic achievements.
As the warriors clashed with each other, their bodies bristled with hair out of the increasing thrill of battle, causing their armor to split or snap under the physical expansion of their excitement.

When the armors were mercilessly slashed by swords, the cotton stuffing inside them flew out into the air. This white cotton filled the sky and all directions, making them appear pale as if covered in gray hair.

The swords of the warriors, smeared with blood yet reflecting the fierce rays of the sun, flashed in every direction. They possessed the splendor and brilliance of lightning bolts amidst the chaos of the fight.
The arrows shot by the enraged warriors seemed like terrifying serpents. Emitting flames from their tips, they streaked across and completely filled the expanse of the sky.
As the archers struck at one another, their arrows pierced through the opponents' bodies with such extreme speed that the tips remained clean of blood as they buried themselves deep into the ground.

In the festive atmosphere of the battle, the arrows of the joyful warriors first pierced through the massive elephants and then struck down the prominent enemy soldiers, causing them to fall to the ground.
As the sky became densely filled with arrows whose tips blazed like fire and were shot at one another, the celestial beings (vaimānikas) traveling high above moved far away to safety.
The sky, pierced by the arrows of the archers, seemed agitated and afflicted with pain; it shrieked harshly under the guise of the screaming echoes of hawks flying through the battlefield.
The arrows, released from bows drawn right back to the ears, sped far across the battlefield as if they were creatures greedy to taste the blood of the warriors seeking combat.
In the battle, the rows of unsheathed swords held by the hands of heroes seemed to laugh out of sheer joy, under the pretext of the flashing net of light reflecting off their blades.
Smeared with blood and dancing in the hands of warriors, the swords displayed the splendor of flashes of lightning amidst the vast battlefield thick with clouds of dust.
On the battlefield, the fierce spears of the warriors flashed as they were brandished, appearing like the darting, flickering tongues of Yama, the God of Death, greedily licking the air.
In the sky of the battlefield, the discs thrown by the expert warriors whirled around, possessing circles of blazing radiance and appearing as beautiful as the orb of the fierce-rayed sun.
Some warriors fell from their mounts due to the agitation caused by the deep roars of the approaching heroes, while others were completely bewildered or fainted out of sheer battle-intoxication.
A certain warrior who loved combat felt great joy when an enemy approached intending to kill him; however, he became despondent when that agitated enemy turned around and retreated from the fight.

Some warriors, fierce in combat, after fighting with many or roaming the field, specifically sought out and approached those particular opponents they had previously chosen to duel with in the battle.
Soldiers, with hair bristling on their powerful arms due to excitement, welcomed the warriors who had approached from all sides to fight, being arrogant with the pride of battle.
Pearls falling down from the frontal globes of elephants split by weapons on the battlefield bore the beauty of sprouted seeds of fame being sown.
Elephants, terrified by the tumultuous shouts of warriors in battle, fled in all directions, shaking off their goads even while being commanded by their mahouts.
Great elephants, pierced by volleys of arrows and reeling after their riders were slain, sank into the rivers formed by the flowing blood on the battlefield.
Even in the shoreless flood of the river of blood, enraged charioteers standing in their high chariots discharged arrows toward the enemy with fierce roars.
Horses whose heads had been severed by swords, even as they were falling, managed to knock down the enemies who had been split apart by swords before they themselves hit the ground.
The heads of warriors, severed by weapons, appeared terrifying as their teeth bit their lips in anger; even while falling, they seemed to rush toward the enemy.
Hawks filled the sky, firmly grasping with their talons the heads of great warriors that had been severed by crescent-shaped arrows.
Foot-soldiers, having climbed onto the tusks of charging elephants in anger, and horse-riders alike destroyed the lives of elephant-riders using their spears.
Elephants whose riders had been killed by weapons wandered aimlessly here and there, appearing like mountains shaken by the cataclysmic winds at the end of an age.
As elephants clashed to fight one another, the warriors, fighting with great force, used their weapons to take each other's lives.
The fire generated by the friction of the tusks of elephants clashing in anger suddenly burnt the warriors, whose lives had already been taken by weapons, along with their enemies.
Even when seized by angry great elephants, the infantrymen managed to take the lives of those elephants with sword strikes, right in front of their own master.
Warriors tossed and released from afar by elephants attained a divine state in heaven via their souls, while their physical bodies reached the earth.
Though the warriors cut off the trunks of elephants with their bright-edged swords and saw them strewn upon the earth, they did not feel satisfied.
Infantrymen, seized by elephant trunks and carried toward heaven (as they died), were quickly sought after by enamoured celestial damsels wanting to receive them.
Archers mounted on horses waited a long time for fainted elephant-riders, whom they had wounded with arrows, to regain consciousness so they could fight them again.
An infantryman, having split the pestle-like tusks of an angry elephant wanting to seize him with its trunk, climbed the animal with the intent to capture it.
A foot-soldier, having hacked off both tusks of an elephant from their roots with his sword, quickly escaped even after having entered deep into the enemy's ranks.
Though firmly grasped by the trunk of an angry elephant, the heroic warrior remained unhurt and quickly took the animal's life with his sword.

A cavalryman struck an opponent mounted on a horse in the chest with a spear. As the opponent was falling, the cavalryman was so absorbed in the act that he did not even realize he himself had been struck by a spear in his own heart.

A warrior, whose life had been taken by an enemy's spear, remained firmly seated on his horse with a large spear still raised in his hand. He moved about the battlefield appearing as if he were still alive.
Even though the great horse was not tied, it did not abandon its rider who had been killed by a weapon and fallen to the ground. Instead, the loyal animal stood by him with eyes full of tears.
A horseman, though pierced by a sharp-edged arrow from the enemy, did not lose consciousness. Driven by intense rage, he still desired to kill his opponent even as he was falling from his horse.

Two warriors, having struck each other with spears and fallen from their horses to the ground, continued to fight in a rage. They engaged in close combat with daggers, pulling each other's hair and fighting hand-to-hand.

Chariot warriors, though killed by the arrows of their opponents, remained firmly seated in their positions. With their bows still held in an aiming posture, they appeared to the observers as if they were still alive.

A righteous chariot warrior did not strike his opponent again when the latter had fainted from weapon wounds. Furthermore, he did not linger on the battlefield out of greed, waiting for the opponent to regain consciousness just to fight him again.
Two chariot warriors killed each other and ascended to heaven. Even there, finding themselves competing for the same celestial nymph, they took up their excellent weapons and continued their duel.

Two chariot warriors, whose heads had been severed by each other's crescent-shaped arrows, ascended to the sky in celestial forms. From their position in the heavens, they looked down and watched their own headless trunks dancing on the battlefield.

On the battlefield, which had become slippery with a mire of blood, rows of headless trunks still clutching their weapons somehow began to dance. This macabre spectacle took place as groups of celestial or ghostly women sang and funeral trumpets blared.

After the battle between the armies of the gods and demons had taken place, wherein the rivers of blood were so deep that herds of elephants were drowning along the banks, the enemy of the gods, Tāraka, became enraged. With eyes turned red and a face terrifyingly distorted by a quivering frown, he instantly approached Indra, the lord of the directions, with an intense desire to engage in combat.

Then, seeing the lord of the Daityas (Tāraka) approaching in front, who was filled with intense joy due to his eagerness for the sport of battle, the lords of the directions reached the mid-air which was darkened by arrows and assembled with passion to fight.

Then the leader of the enemies of the gods, laughing loudly, showered the formidable immortals excessively with rows of arrows, just as a great cloud rains ceaseless and heavy waters upon massive mountains.

The sharp arrows released from the bows of the Dikpālas, led by Indra, instantly and thoroughly shredded the masses of arrows of the Daitya leader into particles, just as groups of Garuḍas tear apart multitudes of serpents.

He (Tāraka), too, covered by floods of arrows that had flaming tips, were deadly, marked with his name, and obscured the sky, destroyed the arrows of the divine army just as fire consumes heaps of grass.
The lord of the Daityas, terrifying with intense anger, effortlessly released arrows in battle that instantly took on the fearsome form of powerful serpents and tightly bound the leaders of the gods.

Bound by the Asura with serpent-noose arrows, their faces distressed by heavy breathing and having turned away from the battle, the lords of directions led by Indra approached the son of Śiva (Kārttikeya) to seek an end to their calamity.

Merely by the falling of the glance of Kārttikeya, Indra and the other gods were spontaneously released from the misery of being tightly bound by the serpent-nooses. Having approached that great one who desired victory, they rendered him their service.

Then Tāraka, the enemy of Indra, whose fierce fire of anger was kindled, quickly spoke to his charioteer: "The gods led by Indra, whom I had forcibly bound, have been freed just by the glance of the young son of Śiva."

"They have now become free; therefore, leaving them aside, I shall make this boy a sacrificial offering on the battlefield. Drive the chariot instantly! I wish to see the strength of the proud arms of Śiva's son in battle."

Instantly driven by the charioteer, that fierce chariot moved forward with a sound as deep and steady as an agitated cloud, its wheels submerged in the thick mud formed by the flesh, bones, and blood of the crushed enemy forces.

Upon seeing the approaching chariot of Tāraka, which was as formidable as a mountain shaken by the winds of destruction and sounded terrifyingly loud, Indra's army, trembling with fear, became intensely agitated.
Observing the army of the gods in turmoil, Tāraka, who looked fierce holding his massive bow, approached Śiva's son, Kārttikeya—who was himself eager for the sport of war—and spoke these words.

Tāraka mocks Kārttikeya, calling him the child of an ascetic and telling him to abandon his pride. He advises him to stop fighting for Indra, questioning what use he has for heavy weapons that are too burdensome for his tender, youthful arms.

Tāraka tells Kārttikeya that as the son of Śiva and Gaurī, he should not seek death by facing his fierce arrows. He urges the boy to retreat from the battlefield and return quickly to the safety of his parents' lap to stay alive.

Tāraka advises Kārttikeya to think carefully and abandon Indra's side. He compares Indra to a stone boat that is already sinking in deep water and warns that he will only pull Kārttikeya down with him.

Hearing Tāraka's words, Kārttikeya became agitated; his lip trembled and his eyes turned red like lotuses. Looking at his bow and considering his own strength, the son of Śiva delivered a fitting reply.

Kārttikeya replies that such boastful talk is expected from the demon king. However, he challenges Tāraka, stating he is ready to see his vaunted strength. He tells the demon to pick up his weapon and ready his bow for combat.

After Kārttikeya spoke, the demon Tāraka, biting his lips in fury, replied to the son of Śiva. He noted that the boy seemed proud of his strength and challenged him to endure his arrows, which had previously forced many enemies to retreat.

Tāraka instantly readied his bow, which was hard for enemies to even look at, and placed fierce arrows upon it. As he aimed his formidable bow and victorious arrows at Kumāra, his weapon resembled a great serpent terrifying in its wrath.

As Tāraka pulled the bowstring all the way back to his ear, the bow discharged a torrent of arrows in every direction. These dense arrows filled the sky like scribes writing across the heavens, seemingly turning all directions white with the intensity of the battle-streaks.

The son of Śiva, Kārttikeya, became invisible to everyone's sight as he was surrounded by countless arrows released from the demon's bow. These arrows, which terrified the soldiers with their roar and emitted clusters of brilliant rays, blinded the entire army of Indra, the lord of the gods.

The divine son of Śiva firmly drew his bow, with its string stretched back to his ear, and discharged sharp, victorious arrows in the battle. By these arrows, the missiles of the demon (the enemy of the gods) were suddenly shattered on all sides.

When the dark storm of the demon's arrows—the cause of distress for all celestial beings—was quickly dispelled, Kārttikeya shone brilliantly. He appeared like the Sun, the lord of light, whose intense splendor is unbearable even for thick clouds.

Then in that battle, the powerful king of demons, who was expert in using illusions, quickly initiated a most unbearable illusory combat against the exceptionally brave and radiant Kumāra, who maintained his composure.

Instantly, the demon Tāraka, turbid with anger yet arrogant due to his world conquests, laughed dreadfully. Deeming Kumāra's excellent weaponry useless, he playfully placed the Vāyavya (wind) missile upon his bow.

As soon as that missile was aimed, a violent wind began to blow, creating the illusion of the end of the world. With a roar terrifying to all, it raised massive clouds of dust that covered the sky and concealed the sun.

Blown away by that fierce wind, the jasmine-white umbrellas of the divine soldiers were scattered across the sky, which was darkened by cloud-like dust. These white umbrellas resembled a flock of graceful swans flying upward.

The great banners of the divine army, white as fresh jasmine, were torn down and carried into the sky by the wind. There, appearing like white garments, they manifested the beauty of thousands of rushing currents of the celestial Gaṅgā.

Hundreds of the great elephants of the divine army, tossed by the wind, with their saddle-blankets torn, instantly fell to the ground in distress. They appeared like the ancient mountains whose wings had been clipped by the thunderbolt of the enraged Indra.

Rows upon rows of chariots belonging to the divine armies were overturned by the fierce wind. With their horses stumbling and falling, and their skilled charioteers thrown off, the chariots spun around and crashed to the ground everywhere.

The riders of the horses in the divine army, distressed by that powerful wind, abandoned their weapons in the midst of the ranks. Even without being struck by any physical weapons, they fell to the ground as their excellent mounts collapsed beneath them.

The infantry of the gods, struck by the wind, dropped their weapons in distress. Screaming harshly and whirling like leaves in a wind-vortex, they were blown far away and fell from the sky onto the surface of the earth.
Seeing the entire divine army thus distressed by the demon king's use of missiles, the great Lord Kārttikeya, who is the sole protector of Indra's prosperity, manifested his divine power.

Upon seeing the army of Indra regain its composure and return to battle after being released from the wind's effect, the demon Tāraka, whose anger blazed like fire, suddenly discharged the flaming Agneyāstra missile.

Thick masses of smoke, resembling the dark clouds at the end of the monsoon and shining like garlands of blue lotuses, instantly spread across the sky. Deeply darkening all directions, they completely destroyed all visibility.

Seeing the sky smeared with dense smoke and darkness that seemed to swallow the horizon, the royal swans were delighted. Mistaking the dark smoke for rain clouds, they immediately desired to fly towards Lake Mānasa.

An incomparable fire, resembling the conflagration at the end of the world, blazed all around the divine soldiers. Its masses of flames turned the clear directions and the entire sky into a reddish-brown hue.
The sky appeared as if filled with clouds of smoke and incessant, incomparable rows of flames from the unrestrained, blazing fire, resembling clusters of lightning.
The entire army of Indra, being intensely scorched by that unbearable and blazing fire which caused even the sky-dwellers to flee, reached the side of Kārttikeya in extreme distress and fear.
Seeing the entire divine army overwhelmed and helpless due to the dense fire, Kārttikeya, the son of Śiva, with a smiling lotus-like face, fitted the Vāruṇa (water) missile onto his bow.

A dense mass of clouds, resembling intense darkness and the thick smoke of the cosmic fire at the end of an eon, rose into the sky. With terrifying thundering roars, it seemed to shatter the very peaks of the mountains.

Then, amidst the clouds in the sky, lightning flashed brilliantly with deep, terrifying thunders. Turning the directions dark, it appeared like the flickering, fearsome tongue of Kāla (Time or Death) stirred into action at the end of the world.

The bank of clouds shone in the sky, lighting up the directions with lightning while obstructing all vision. With their uneven and terrifying thunders, they resembled the rows of dark clouds during the night of destruction or the dark-throated form of Lord Śiva.

The masses of clouds, covering the entire sky and the faces of all directions, began to rain heavily everywhere. Their ceaseless thundering agitated the minds of all as they poured down thick, substantial streams of water.

The all-consuming fire, which filled the entire universe, was extinguished by the rain from the clouds produced by the Varuṇa weapon. These clouds covered the sky in thick darkness and distressed the demons with their deep, heavy thundering.

Filled with rage, the demon Tāraka drew his bow to his ear and discharged sharp, terrifying crescent-shaped arrows. He forcefully struck Kārttikeya (the son of Śiva), whose entire divine army had already fled in terror of the demon.

Lord Kārttikeya, treating the battle as sport, used his arrows to cut the demon's bow and multitude of arrows into tiny pieces. He did this just as a yogi, whose mind is disciplined by yoga practice, destroys the powerful and distracting collection of worldly sense-objects using self-restraint.

Then the emperor of demons, his face terrifying with knitted brows and a blazing fire of anger, abandoned his chariot. Brandishing a fearsome sword in his hand, he charged directly towards Kārttikeya, the son of Lord Śiva.

Seeing the demon king charging with irresistible strength—a sight that terrified the divine soldiers—Kārttikeya remained calm. With a joyful, blooming lotus-like face, he released his Śakti spear, which shone with the intensity of the cosmic fire that ends an eon.

The Śakti spear, illuminating the sky and every direction with its brilliant rays, struck the great demon Tāraka right in the heart. Its impact was accompanied simultaneously by the joyful tears of the lords of the universe and the hot tears of grief from the demons.

Upon seeing the lord of demons falling, his life extinguished by the spear like a mountain peak shattered by cosmic winds at the end of an aeon, the gods led by Indra felt immense joy, their beautiful bodies covered in horripilation from excitement.

As the lifeless king of demons fell like a massive mountain collapsing during the dissolution of the universe, the lord of serpents, Śeṣa, used his hoods to support the earth, which was sinking downwards under the immense weight of the fallen giant.

A rain of flowers from the celestial Kalpa trees, moistened by the spray of the heavenly Ganges and surrounded by bees attracted to their scent, showered from the sky onto the head of Kārttikeya, the son of Śiva and the vanquisher of the gods' foe.

All the divine hosts led by Indra, their faces glowing with joy and their armor bursting from the physical thrill of victory, celebrated the extraordinary power of Kārttikeya's arms, who had just defeated the demon Tāraka.

After the victorious son of Śiva removed the king of demons, who was a thorn to the three worlds, Indra regained his sovereignty over heaven and triumphed, with the tips of his feet being touched by the jewels of the bowing gods' crowns.
